runs.prompt: what is cross entropy
runs.title: Cross-Entropy Loss
runs.body:
Cross-entropy measures the difference between two probability distributions, typically the true labels $y$ and the predicted probabilities $p$.

For a single binary classification instance, the formula is $H(y,p) = -y \log(p) - (1-y) \log(1-p)$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Cross-entropy loss curves","caption":"Loss grows as the predicted probability moves away from the true class label.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Predicted probability $p$","min":0,"max":1},"y":{"label":"Loss","min":0,"max":5},"series":[{"label":"$y=1$","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":4.605},{"x":0.25,"y":1.386},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":0.288},{"x":0.99,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"$y=0$","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":0.01},{"x":0.25,"y":0.288},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":1.386},{"x":0.99,"y":4.605}]}]}}
```

When the true label is $y=1$, the loss simplifies to $-\log(p)$, heavily penalizing predictions where $p$ approaches zero.

Conversely, if $y=0$, the loss becomes $-\log(1-p)$, penalizing confident incorrect predictions near $p=1$.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy
runs.title: Cross-Entropy Loss
runs.body:
Cross-entropy measures the difference between two probability distributions, typically the true labels $y$ and the predicted probabilities $p$.

For a single binary decision, the formula is $H(y,p) = -y \log p - (1-y) \log (1-p)$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Cross-entropy loss curves","caption":"Loss grows as predicted probability diverges from the true label.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Predicted positive probability","min":0.01,"max":0.99},"y":{"label":"Loss","min":0,"max":5},"series":[{"label":"True class 1","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":4.605},{"x":0.25,"y":1.386},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":0.288},{"x":0.99,"y":0.01,"label":"(0.99, 0.01)"}]},{"label":"True class 0","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":0.01,"label":"(0.01, 0.01)"},{"x":0.25,"y":0.288},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":1.386},{"x":0.99,"y":4.605}]}]}}
```

The plot shows how penalty increases exponentially when the model assigns high confidence to the wrong class.

If the true class is $1$ and the model predicts $p=0.99$, the loss is near zero, but predicting $p=0.01$ incurs a massive penalty.

In practice, minimizing this objective via gradient descent drives the predicted distribution to match the empirical data distribution.

Its main failure mode is extreme sensitivity to outliers when probabilities approach exact bounds.

runs.prompt: what is gradient descent?
runs.title: Gradient Descent Optimization
runs.body:
Gradient descent is an iterative optimization algorithm used to minimize a cost function $L(w)$. The parameter update rule is given by $w_{t+1} = w_t - \alpha \nabla L(w_t)$, where $\alpha$ is the learning rate.

Look at the vectors in the plot showing how steps descend toward the minimum.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"A descent path on a quadratic loss","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Weight 1","min":-3,"max":3,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Weight 2","min":-3,"max":3},"series":[{"label":"Outer loss contour","kind":"line","closed":true,"samples":{"radius":2,"count":16}},{"label":"Inner loss contour","kind":"line","closed":true,"samples":{"radius":1,"count":16}}],"annotations":[{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 1","from":{"x":-1.5,"y":1.1},"to":{"x":-0.9,"y":0.7}},{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 2","from":{"x":-0.9,"y":0.7},"to":{"x":-0.4,"y":0.3}},{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 3","from":{"x":-0.4,"y":0.3},"to":{"x":0,"y":0}}]}}
```

Choosing the correct learning rate $\alpha$ is critical in practice. If $\alpha$ is too large, the updates can overshoot the minimum and diverge; if it is too small, training becomes excessively slow.

runs.prompt: what is gradient descent?
runs.title: Gradient Descent Optimization
runs.body:
Gradient descent is an iterative optimization algorithm used to find the minimum of a differentiable function $L(w)$.

The parameter updates follow the rule $w_{t+1} = w_t - \eta \nabla L(w_t)$, where $\eta$ represents the learning rate scalar step size.

Look at Step 1, Step 2, and Step 3 in the coordinate plot to see how successive parameter vectors travel orthogonally across loss contours.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"A descent path on a quadratic loss","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Weight 1","min":-3,"max":3,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Weight 2","min":-3,"max":3},"series":[{"label":"Outer loss contour","kind":"line","closed":true,"samples":{"radius":2,"count":16}},{"label":"Inner loss contour","kind":"line","closed":true,"samples":{"radius":1,"count":16}}],"annotations":[{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 1","from":{"x":-1.5,"y":1.1},"to":{"x":-0.9,"y":0.7}},{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 2","from":{"x":-0.9,"y":0.7},"to":{"x":-0.4,"y":0.3}},{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 3","from":{"x":-0.4,"y":0.3},"to":{"x":0,"y":0}}]}}
```

The choice of the learning rate $\eta$ governs convergence stability; too large a value causes divergence, whereas too small a value stalls progress.

In practice, failure modes include getting trapped in local minima or saddle points where the gradient vanishes.

runs.prompt: what is a learning rate schedule?
runs.title: Learning Rate Schedules
runs.body:
A learning rate schedule dynamically adjusts the step size $\alpha_t$ during training to balance rapid initial convergence with stable fine-tuning near a minimum.

Notice how the step decay drops sharply at set epochs while exponential decay scales smoothly.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Learning-rate schedules share an epoch axis","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Epoch","min":0,"max":6,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Learning rate","min":0.001,"max":0.1,"scale":"log"},"series":[{"label":"Step decay","kind":"step","points":[{"x":0,"y":0.1},{"x":2,"y":0.03},{"x":4,"y":0.01},{"x":6,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"Exponential decay","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0.1},{"x":1,"y":0.05},{"x":2,"y":0.025},{"x":3,"y":0.0125},{"x":4,"y":0.00625},{"x":5,"y":0.003125},{"x":6,"y":0.0015625}]}],"annotations":[]}}
```

Formally, exponential decay follows $\alpha_t = \alpha_0 \gamma^t$, where $\alpha_0$ is the initial rate and $\gamma$ is the decay factor per epoch $t$.

Choosing an improper decay rate causes either premature stalling or violent parameter oscillations.

runs.prompt: what is a learning rate schedule?
runs.title: Learning-Rate Schedules in Training
runs.body:
A learning rate schedule dynamically scales step size during gradient descent optimization. By decreasing the rate over time, training avoids overshooting optimal minima as gradients become small.

Look at step decay and exponential decay curves plotted against epochs in above.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Learning-rate schedules over epochs","caption":"Step decay drops the rate at fixed intervals, while exponential decay drops it continuously.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Epoch","min":0,"max":6,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Learning rate","min":0.001,"max":0.1,"scale":"log"},"series":[{"label":"Step decay","kind":"step","points":[{"x":0,"y":0.1},{"x":2,"y":0.03},{"x":4,"y":0.01},{"x":6,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"Exponential decay","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0.1},{"x":1,"y":0.05},{"x":2,"y":0.025},{"x":3,"y":0.0125},{"x":4,"y":0.00625},{"x":5,"y":0.003125},{"x":6,"y":0.0015625}]}],"annotations":[]}}
```

Step decay reduces the rate by a factor $\gamma$ every $k$ epochs according to $\alpha_t = \alpha_0 \gamma^{\lfloor t / k \rfloor}$. Exponential decay updates every epoch via $\alpha_t = \alpha_0 \gamma^t$.

A common failure mode in practice is setting decay rates too aggressively, which stalls convergence before reaching the true minimum.

runs.title: Precision and Recall
runs.body:
Precision measures how many selected items are relevant, while recall measures how many relevant items are selected.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Precision vs Recall Confusion Matrix","caption":"Columns show actual classes, rows show predicted classes.","kind":"matrix","layout":"teaching","columns":["Actual Positive","Actual Negative"],"rows":[{"id":"predicted-positive","heading":"Predicted Positive","cells":["True Positive","False Positive"]},{"id":"predicted-negative","heading":"Predicted Negative","cells":["False Negative","True Negative"]}]}}
```

Precision uses predicted positives as its denominator, defined as $\frac{\text{True Positives}}{\text{True Positives} + \text{False Positives}}$.

Recall uses actual positives as its denominator, defined as $\frac{\text{True Positives}}{\text{True Positives} + \text{False Negatives}}$.

runs.prompt: what is the difference between precision and recall?
runs.title: Precision vs Recall
runs.body:
Precision is the fraction of retrieved instances that are relevant, defined as $\frac{TP}{TP + FP}$. It measures the accuracy of positive predictions.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Confusion Matrix","caption":"Precision focuses on column totals while recall focuses on row totals.","kind":"matrix","columns":["Predicted Positive","Predicted Negative"],"rows":[{"heading":"Actual Positive","cells":["True Positive (TP)","False Negative (FN)"]},{"heading":"Actual Negative","cells":["False Positive (FP)","True Negative (TN)"]}]}}
```

Recall is the fraction of relevant instances that were retrieved, defined as $\frac{TP}{TP + FN}$. It measures the ability to find all positive instances.

There is a trade-off between them because increasing the decision threshold raises precision and lowers recall.

runs.prompt: what does the sigmoid activation function do?
runs.title: The Sigmoid Activation Function
runs.body:
The sigmoid function maps any real-valued number into a strict range between $0$ and $1$. Its exact formula is $\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$, where $z$ represents the linear score from a model.

Look for the S-shaped curve and the threshold lines at $0.5$ in the plot below to see how inputs scale.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"A sigmoid links score to probability","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Linear score","min":-4,"max":4,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Positive probability","min":0,"max":1},"series":[{"label":"Sigmoid","kind":"line","points":[{"x":-4,"y":0.018},{"x":-3,"y":0.047},{"x":-2,"y":0.119},{"x":-1,"y":0.269},{"x":0,"y":0.5},{"x":1,"y":0.731},{"x":2,"y":0.881},{"x":3,"y":0.953},{"x":4,"y":0.982}]}],"annotations":[{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Probability threshold","axis":"y","value":0.5},{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Equivalent score threshold","axis":"x","value":0}]}}
```

This squashing property allows outputs to be interpreted directly as probabilities in binary classification tasks.

A major limitation in practice is vanishing gradients, where extreme inputs push the derivative near zero and stall learning.

runs.prompt: what does the sigmoid activation function do?
runs.title: The Sigmoid Activation Function
runs.body:
The sigmoid activation function maps any real-valued number into a bounded range between $0$ and $1$.

Its exact form is defined by the formula $\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$, where $z$ represents the incoming linear score.

Observe how the curve squashes extreme positive and negative inputs into probabilities, centered at an output of $0.5$ when $z = 0$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"A sigmoid links score to probability","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Linear score","min":-4,"max":4,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Positive probability","min":0,"max":1},"series":[{"label":"Sigmoid","kind":"line","points":[{"x":-4,"y":0.018},{"x":-3,"y":0.047},{"x":-2,"y":0.119},{"x":-1,"y":0.269},{"x":0,"y":0.5},{"x":1,"y":0.731},{"x":2,"y":0.881},{"x":3,"y":0.953},{"x":4,"y":0.982}]}],"annotations":[{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Probability threshold","axis":"y","value":0.5},{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Equivalent score threshold","axis":"x","value":0}]}}
```

In practice, this mapping allows neural networks to interpret raw scores as probabilities for binary classification tasks.

A major limitation of the function is vanishing gradients, where deep layers stall because the derivative $\sigma'(z)$ approaches zero as inputs grow large in either direction.

runs.prompt: what does softmax do?
runs.title: Softmax Activation Function
runs.body:
The softmax function transforms a vector of arbitrary real-valued scores into a probability distribution.

It takes unconstrained inputs called logits and maps them so that every output lies strictly between $0$ and $1$, and all outputs sum to $1$. Look at the input values and their mapped probabilities in the diagram below.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Logits to Probabilities via Softmax","caption":"Raw scores $z_i$ are exponentiated and divided by the sum to form probabilities $\\sigma(z)_i$.","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Logits","items":["z_1 = 2.0","z_2 = 1.0","z_3 = 0.1"]},"after":{"label":"Probabilities","items":["0.66","0.24","0.10"]},"operation":"Apply sigma(z)_i = exp(z_i) / sum(exp(z_j))"}}
```

The precise formula for the $i$-th element is $\sigma(z)_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j} e^{z_j}}$. The exponential numerator magnifies differences between inputs, making the largest logit dominate the distribution.

In practice, practitioners subtract the maximum logit from all inputs before exponentiation to prevent numerical overflow during computation.

runs.prompt: what does softmax do?
runs.title: Softmax Function Transformation
runs.body:
The softmax function turns a vector of raw scores, called logits, into a proper probability distribution where all values lie in the open interval $(0, 1)$ and sum exactly to $1$.

Look for the exponential scaling and normalization steps in the transformation diagram below.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Converting logits to probabilities","caption":"The softmax function scales raw scores into a probability distribution summing to one.","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Logits","items":["$z_1 = 2.0$","$z_2 = 1.0$","$z_3 = 0.1$"]},"after":{"label":"Probabilities","items":["$p_1 = 0.66$","$p_2 = 0.24$","$p_3 = 0.10$"]},"operation":"Apply $\\sigma(z)_i = \\frac{e^{z_i}}{\\sum_j e^{z_j}}$"}}
```

Given an input vector $z$, the probability for the $i$-th class is defined as $p_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j} e^{z_j}}$.

The exponential numerator magnifies differences between scores, making the highest logit stand out more strongly.

A primary limitation in practice is numerical overflow when logits are very large positive numbers.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy
runs.title: Cross Entropy
runs.body:
Imagine guessing whether a coin landed on heads or tails based on a friend's hints. Cross entropy is a score that measures how surprised you are by those guesses compared to what actually happened.

When a model makes a prediction, this score tells us how wrong the guess is.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Comparing Real and Predicted Outcomes","kind":"comparison","columns":[{"heading":"True Label","items":["The actual event that happened","Stored as a 1 or 0"]},{"heading":"Predicted Probability","items":["The guess made by the model","A number between 0 and 1"]}]}}
```

Think of the true answer as a 1 for the correct event and 0 for everything else. The model assigns a probability to each option, representing its confidence.

Cross entropy takes the logarithm of that predicted probability when the event actually occurs. If the model is confident and correct, the penalty is tiny.

If it is confident and wrong, the penalty shoots up toward infinity.

runs.body:
Imagine you are standing on a foggy hill and want to reach the lowest valley. You can feel the slope with your feet to figure out which way is down.

You take a step in that direction and repeat the process until the ground feels flat.

This walking process is what gradient descent does for computer algorithms. The hill represents an error function, where high points mean many mistakes and the bottom means zero errors.

By checking the slope, the algorithm adjusts its settings to reduce errors step by step.

By moving in the opposite direction, the computer reduces errors and improves its guesses.

runs.prompt: what is the difference between precision and recall?
runs.title: Precision vs Recall
runs.body:
Imagine you are sorting out spam emails from your inbox. Precision asks how many of the emails you flagged as spam were actually spam. If you label ten emails as spam and nine are truly spam, your precision is high.

Recall asks how many of all the actual spam emails in your inbox you managed to catch. If there were twenty spam emails total and you found ten of them, your recall is fifty percent.

```rh-diagram

```

To see this clearly, look at the matrix above showing the outcomes of a classifier. Precision focuses on the top-left cell divided by the top row. Recall focuses on the top-left cell divided by the left column.

There is a trade-off between the two metrics.

runs.prompt: what is the difference between precision and recall?

Recall tells you how many of the real spam messages in your inbox the filter managed to catch. If spam still slips through, the recall is low. The matrix above shows how these two ideas use correct and incorrect guesses.

Precision worries about false alarms, while recall worries about missed items. Balancing them is key for a good test.

The true label $y$ is either $0$ or $1$, defining the penalty function.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Cross-entropy depends on the true label","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Predicted positive probability","min":0.01,"max":0.99,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Loss","min":0,"max":5},"series":[{"label":"True class 1","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":4.605},{"x":0.1,"y":2.303},{"x":0.25,"y":1.386},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":0.288},{"x":0.9,"y":0.105},{"x":0.99,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"True class 0","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":0.01},{"x":0.1,"y":0.105},{"x":0.25,"y":0.288},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":1.386},{"x":0.9,"y":2.303},{"x":0.99,"y":4.605}]}],"annotations":[]}}
```

When the true label is $1$, the loss is $-\log(p)$, meaning a prediction near zero incurs massive penalty. Conversely, when the true label is $0$, the loss becomes $-\log(1-p)$.

This logarithmic scoring rule drives optimal model training.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy
runs.title: Cross-Entropy Loss
runs.body:
Cross-entropy measures the difference between two probability distributions, typically the true labels and predicted outputs.

In classification models, it penalizes confident and wrong predictions heavily using a logarithmic scale.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Cross-entropy loss by predicted probability","caption":"Loss grows as prediction diverges from true label.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Predicted probability p","min":0.01,"max":0.99},"y":{"label":"Loss","min":0,"max":5},"series":[{"label":"True class 1","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":4.61},{"x":0.25,"y":1.39},{"x":0.5,"y":0.69},{"x":0.75,"y":0.29},{"x":0.99,"y":0.01}]}]}}
```

The formula for a single binary instance is $H(y, p) = -(y \log(p) + (1 - y) \log(1 - p))$, where $y$ is the true label and $p$ is the predicted probability.

As the model's prediction approaches the correct label, the loss approaches zero.

When the model assigns a low probability to the correct class, the $-\log(p)$ term shoots up toward infinity, driving up the overall loss. This penalty guides gradient descent to adjust model weights effectively.

runs.prompt: what is gradient descent?
runs.title: Gradient Descent
runs.body:
Gradient descent is an iterative optimisation algorithm used to find the minimum of a function by adjusting parameters in the direction of steepest descent.

Suppose we want to minimise a quadratic loss function $L(w) = w^2$ starting from an initial weight $w = -2$.

The algorithm computes the derivative of the loss with respect to the weight, known as the gradient, which tells us the slope at our current position.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Gradient Descent Path","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the steps toward the minimum.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Weight","min":-3,"max":3,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Loss","min":0,"max":9},"series":[{"label":"$Loss = w^2$","kind":"line","points":[{"x":-3,"y":9},{"x":-2,"y":4},{"x":-1,"y":1},{"x":0,"y":0},{"x":1,"y":1},{"x":2,"y":4},{"x":3,"y":9}]}],"annotations":[{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 1","from":{"x":-2,"y":4},"to":{"x":-1,"y":1}},{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 2","from":{"x":-1,"y":1},"to":{"x":-0.3,"y":0.09}}]}}
```

To update the weight, we take a small step proportional to this slope, scaled by a hyperparameter called the learning rate.

If the learning rate is too large, the updates overshoot the minimum; if it is too small, convergence takes too many steps.

Gradient descent is an iterative optimization algorithm used to find the minimum of a function by adjusting parameters in the direction of steepest descent.

Suppose we train a model with an initial parameter set yielding high error, measured by a cost function $J(w)$.

Choosing an appropriate learning rate ensures the model converges efficiently without overshooting the minimum.

runs.prompt: what is a learning rate schedule?
runs.title: Learning Rate Schedule
runs.body:
Training a neural network requires adjusting the step size over time to converge smoothly. A learning rate schedule controls this adjustment by reducing the learning rate during training.

Observe the curve geometry and step drops in as training epochs advance.


runs.prompt: what is the difference between precision and recall?
runs.title: Precision vs Recall
runs.body:
Precision and recall measure a classification model's performance by focusing on different types of errors.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Confusion Matrix for Classification","kind":"matrix","columns":["Predicted Positive","Predicted Negative"],"rows":[{"heading":"Actual Positive","cells":["True Positive (TP)","False Negative (FN)"]},{"heading":"Actual Negative","cells":["False Positive (FP)","True Negative (TN)"]}]}}
```

Precision calculates how many predicted positives are actually correct, using the formula $\frac{TP}{TP + FP}$. Recall measures how many actual positives the model managed to capture, using $\frac{TP}{TP + FN}$.

runs.prompt: what is the difference between precision and recall?
runs.title: Precision vs Recall
runs.body:
When evaluating a classifier, precision and recall measure different kinds of errors. Consider a medical test that flags a rare disease. Precision asks: out of all positive predictions, how many were actually correct?

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Confusion matrix counts","kind":"matrix","columns":["Predicted Positive","Predicted Negative"],"rows":[{"heading":"Actual Positive","cells":["True Positive","False Negative"]},{"heading":"Actual Negative","cells":["False Positive","True Negative"]}]}}
```

Recall asks: out of all actual positive cases, how many did the model manage to find? Precision guards against false alarms, while recall guards against missed detections.

runs.prompt: what does the sigmoid activation function do?
runs.title: The Sigmoid Activation Function
runs.body:
Suppose a model predicts whether an email is spam by combining features into a single number called a linear score.

Because this raw score can range from negative to positive infinity, we need a way to squash it into a valid probability. The sigmoid function takes any real-valued number and maps it strictly between zero and one.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"A sigmoid links score to probability","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Linear score","min":-4,"max":4,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Positive probability","min":0,"max":1},"series":[{"label":"Sigmoid","kind":"line","points":[{"x":-4,"y":0.018},{"x":-3,"y":0.047},{"x":-2,"y":0.119},{"x":-1,"y":0.269},{"x":0,"y":0.5},{"x":1,"y":0.731},{"x":2,"y":0.881},{"x":3,"y":0.953},{"x":4,"y":0.982}]}],"annotations":[{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Probability threshold","axis":"y","value":0.5},{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Equivalent score threshold","axis":"x","value":0}]}}
```

Looking at the S-shaped curve above, notice how extreme negative scores approach zero and extreme positive scores approach one.

The formula is defined as $\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$, where $z$ is the incoming score. When the input score is zero, the output probability is exactly half.

runs.prompt: what does the sigmoid activation function do?
runs.title: The Sigmoid Activation Function
runs.body:
In logistic regression, a linear model outputs a raw score that can range from negative to positive infinity. This unbounded value makes direct probabilistic interpretation difficult for classification tasks.

To fix this, we apply the sigmoid function to squeeze the score into a clean range between zero and one.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"A sigmoid links score to probability","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Linear score","min":-4,"max":4,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Positive probability","min":0,"max":1},"series":[{"label":"Sigmoid","kind":"line","points":[{"x":-4,"y":0.018},{"x":-3,"y":0.047},{"x":-2,"y":0.119},{"x":-1,"y":0.269},{"x":0,"y":0.5},{"x":1,"y":0.731},{"x":2,"y":0.881},{"x":3,"y":0.953},{"x":4,"y":0.982}]}],"annotations":[{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Probability threshold","axis":"y","value":0.5},{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Equivalent score threshold","axis":"x","value":0}]}}
```

The sigmoid formula is defined as $\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$, where $z$ represents the incoming linear score. When the score is zero, the function outputs exactly $0.5$.

Extremely positive scores approach $1.0$, while extremely negative scores approach $0.0$.

This S-shaped curve acts as a squashing gate that interprets outputs as probabilities.

runs.prompt: what is gini impurity
runs.title: Gini Impurity Formula
runs.body:
Gini impurity measures how often a randomly chosen element from a set would be incorrectly labeled if it were randomly labeled according to the distribution of labels in the subset.

For $J$ classes, the formal definition is $I_G(p) = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{J} p_i^2$, where $p_i$ is the probability of a randomly chosen item belonging to class $i$.

Look for the peak at probability $0.5$ in the plot to see where uncertainty is highest for a binary split.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Gini Impurity for Binary Classification","caption":"Impurity reaches its maximum of 0.5 when classes are perfectly balanced at $p=0.5$.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Probability $p$","min":0,"max":1},"y":{"label":"Gini Impurity $I_G(p)$","min":0,"max":0.6},"series":[{"label":"$1 - p^2 - (1-p)^2$","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0},{"x":0.2,"y":0.32},{"x":0.4,"y":0.48},{"x":0.5,"y":0.5,"label":"$(0.5, 0.5)$"},{"x":0.6,"y":0.48},{"x":0.8,"y":0.32},{"x":1,"y":0}]}]}}
```

In decision trees, algorithms compute this metric across candidate splits to choose the feature threshold that minimizes child node impurity.

runs.prompt: how are attention weights computed?

runs.prompt: what does softmax do?
runs.title: Softmax Activation Function
runs.body:
Softmax turns raw model scores into a valid probability distribution that sums to one. For instance, classification models output unconstrained numbers called logits for each class.

Look at how the raw values are exponentiated and scaled relative to each other in

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Softmax Transformation","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Logits","items":["2.0","1.0","0.1"]},"after":{"label":"Probabilities","items":["0.66","0.24","0.10"]},"operation":"Apply exponential and normalize by sum"}}
```

.

The softmax function takes an input vector of real numbers and applies the standard exponential function to each component.

Because exponential growth magnifies differences, larger logits receive exponentially larger weights before division.

Dividing each exponentiated value by the sum of all exponentiated values forces the final outputs to lie strictly between zero and one.

runs.prompt: what does softmax do?
runs.title: Softmax Activation Function
runs.body:
Neural networks output raw scores called logits for each possible class. These scores can be any real number and do not sum to one.

Look at how raw scores change in the transformation diagram.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Converting logits to probabilities with softmax","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Logits","items":["2.0","1.0","0.1"]},"after":{"label":"Probabilities","items":["0.70","0.26","0.04"]},"operation":"Apply exponentiate and normalize"}}
```

The softmax function turns these raw logits into valid probabilities that sum to one. It exponentiates each score to make it positive and divides by the sum of all exponentiated scores.

This amplification highlights the largest logit while suppressing smaller ones, making it ideal for multi-class classification.

runs.prompt: What happens to a skewed distribution when we take logs?
runs.title: Taking logs of a skewed distribution
runs.body:
When data has a long right tail, taking logarithms pulls the largest values inward. Consider a financial dataset where most values cluster near zero but a few stretch far out.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Comparing raw and log scales","caption":"Log transformation compresses the long right tail, pulling large values closer while stretching small values.","kind":"comparison","columns":[{"heading":"Raw values","items":["Right-skewed mass","Long tail on the right","High variance in scale","Multiplicative effects"]},{"heading":"Log values","items":["Compressed right tail","Symmetrical spread","Reduced scale variance","Additive effects"]}]}}
```

This logarithmic transformation compresses the right tail while expanding the lower scale. Multiplicative changes become additive shifts, making relationships easier to analyze.

While this compression often makes distributions look more bell-shaped, logs do not guarantee normality. Every raw value must be positive, and zeroes require a small offset like $\log(1+x)$.

runs.prompt: What happens to a skewed distribution when we take logs?
runs.title: Skewed Distributions and Log Transformations
runs.body:
When data spans multiple orders of magnitude with a long right tail, a log transformation pulls in those extreme high values. This makes the spread more symmetric and stabilizes variance across the range.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Raw and Log Distributions","kind":"comparison","columns":[{"heading":"Raw Scale","items":["Right-skewed tail","Large variance","Compressed low values"]},{"heading":"Log Scale","items":["Symmetric spread","Stabilized variance","Expanded low values"]}]}}
```

By applying a logarithmic function, multiplicative effects become additive ones. This reshaping helps many statistical models meet their core assumptions.

However, logs cannot handle zero or negative values without an offset like $log(x + 1)$. Interpretation also shifts because differences on the log scale represent percentage changes in the original units.

runs.prompt: How does Bayesian optimization decide which setting to try next?
runs.title: How Bayesian Optimization Picks the Next Trial

Bayesian optimization uses a surrogate model to predict performance across unknown hyperparameter settings. This model outputs both a predicted mean and an uncertainty value for each candidate setting.

```rh-diagram

```

An acquisition function then combines these two values into a single score. Notice how candidate C achieves the highest overall score because its high uncertainty bonus outweighs its slightly lower mean.

This balance lets the optimizer choose between exploiting known good regions and exploring uncertain new areas.

runs.prompt: How does Bayesian optimization decide which setting to try next?

Bayesian optimization balances exploring unknown regions and exploiting known good settings by building a probabilistic model of the objective function.

Look for the highest score in the rightmost column of the matrix, which combines predicted performance and uncertainty to select the next trial.

An acquisition function such as the upper confidence bound calculates a score by adding an uncertainty bonus to the mean, rewarding both high predicted performance and regions with high variance.

runs.prompt: what is entropy?
runs.title: Entropy in Thermodynamics
runs.body:
Thermodynamic entropy is a state function that measures the unavailability of a system's thermal energy for conversion into mechanical work.

Look at the diagram below to see how a reversible heat transfer changes this state function.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Entropy change in a reversible process","caption":"The entropy change $dS$ is defined by the heat transferred at temperature $T$.","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Initial Macrostate","items":["Energy $U$","Temperature $T$"]},"after":{"label":"Final Macrostate","items":["Energy $U + dQ$","Entropy $dS = \\frac{dQ}{T}$"]},"operation":"Add reversible heat $dQ$"}}
```

Quantitatively, the change in entropy $dS$ is given by the exact differential $dS = \frac{dQ_{\text{rev}}}{T}$, where $dQ_{\text{rev}}$ is the heat added reversibly and $T$ is the absolute temperature.

For any natural spontaneous process in an isolated system, the total entropy change is strictly greater than zero, expressing the second law of thermodynamics.

runs.prompt: what is entropy?
runs.title: Entropy in Thermodynamics
runs.body:
Entropy is a measure of the number of microscopic configurations corresponding to a macroscopic thermodynamic system.

It is defined precisely by Boltzmann's formula $S = k_B \ln \Omega$, where $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant and $\Omega$ is the multiplicity of microstates.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"State transition increasing entropy","caption":"Transition from an ordered microstate to a disordered macrostate showing an increase in $S$.","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Ordered state","items":["Low multiplicity $\\Omega$"]},"after":{"label":"Disordered state","items":["High multiplicity $\\Omega$"]},"operation":"Allow thermal expansion"}}
```

In any isolated system, spontaneous processes drive the system toward a state of maximum multiplicity.

This principle is governed by the second law of thermodynamics, which states that the total entropy can never decrease over time for an isolated system.

A key limitation in practice is that calculating $\Omega$ directly for macroscopic systems containing Avogadro's number of particles is intractable.

Starting with an initial principal of $1,000 at a 10% annual rate, interest applies to both the original amount and accumulated earnings.

When you invest money, compound interest lets your earnings generate their own earnings over time.

Think of depositing $1,000 at an annual rate of 8% interest. After the first year, you earn $80, bringing your total to $1,080.

Look at the exponential curve to see how the slope steepens as the years increase.

runs.title: Population Growth Models
runs.body:
Populations start growing slowly when individuals are few, then speed up as more parents reproduce. This unrestricted expansion follows an exponential curve where growth depends on the per capita birth rate $r$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Exponential vs Logistic Growth","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Time","min":0,"max":7},"y":{"label":"Population","min":0,"max":120},"series":[{"label":"Exponential","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":10},{"x":1,"y":14},{"x":2,"y":20},{"x":3,"y":28},{"x":4,"y":40},{"x":5,"y":56},{"x":6,"y":80},{"x":7,"y":113}]},{"label":"Logistic","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":10},{"x":1,"y":18},{"x":2,"y":32},{"x":3,"y":50,"label":"K/2"},{"x":4,"y":70},{"x":5,"y":85},{"x":6,"y":93},{"x":7,"y":97}]}]}}
```

In real environments, resources become scarce and limit further expansion.

This braking effect introduces carrying capacity $K$, bending the curve into a logistic shape where growth slows down as population size approaches the maximum sustainable limit.

The logistic growth rate is given by the differential equation $\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(\frac{K-N}{K}\right)$, which reduces growth to zero when $N$ equals $K$.

runs.prompt: how do populations grow?
runs.title: Population Growth Models
runs.body:
When resources are unlimited, populations expand through exponential growth where the rate of increase is proportional to the current population size.

This pattern follows the differential equation $\frac{dN}{dt} = rN$, producing a J-shaped curve when plotted against time.


As individuals multiply faster and faster, the curve steepens sharply because every new member contributes to further reproduction.

Here, $r$ represents the per capita growth rate, and $N$ denotes the total number of individuals in the habitat.

In real environments, this unchecked expansion eventually collides with limiting factors like food scarcity or disease, shifting growth toward a stable carrying capacity.

runs.prompt: what is overfitting?
runs.title: Understanding Overfitting
runs.body:
When a machine learning model learns the training data too well, including its noise and random fluctuations, it suffers from overfitting.

This happens when a model has high capacity and captures spurious patterns instead of the underlying general rule. Consequently, its performance on new, unseen data degrades significantly.

Notice the training points and the held-out point on the plot below, comparing a smooth linear model to a jagged high-degree curve.

In contrast, the overfit curve contorts wildly to pass through every training point, missing the held-out test point entirely.

runs.title: Quantization in Neural Networks
runs.body:
Consider converting a continuous model weight of $3.1415$ into a compact 8-bit integer to save memory.

Quantization is the process of mapping continuous infinite values to a smaller set of discrete values, reducing memory footprints.

runs.prompt: what is quantization?
runs.title: What is Quantization?
runs.body:
Quantization maps a continuous range of values into a discrete set of fixed steps. Consider converting a smooth analog audio wave into digital samples by rounding each voltage to the nearest allowed integer level.

This process introduces quantization error, which is the difference between the original value and its rounded counterpart.

```rh-diagram

```

In machine learning, quantization reduces the precision of model weights, such as converting 32-bit floating-point numbers to 8-bit integers.

This transformation shrinks memory footprints and speeds up inference while preserving most of the original model accuracy. The mapping is defined by a scaling factor and a zero-point offset to fit the numeric range.

Tokenization converts raw text into smaller pieces called tokens so a language model can process them. Algorithms like Byte-Pair Encoding merge frequent character pairs iteratively until a fixed vocabulary is reached.

Look at the diagram above to see how a single word splits into subword pieces and maps to numeric IDs. Each token is then looked up in an embedding matrix to get a vector representation.

runs.prompt: what is a vector database?
runs.title: Vector Databases
runs.body:
A vector database indexes high-dimensional numeric arrays called embeddings, which capture semantic meaning from text, images, or audio.

When a query arrives, the system computes geometric distance to find the nearest neighbours.

Look at the coordinate plot to see how items with similar meanings cluster together in space.

```rh-diagram

```

Unlike traditional databases that match exact strings, a vector database uses approximate nearest neighbour search to retrieve conceptually related records.

This capability powers modern semantic search, recommendation systems, and retrieval-augmented generation in artificial intelligence applications.

runs.prompt: what is a vector database?
runs.title: Vector Database Mechanism
runs.body:
When searching for similar images or text, a vector database indexes high-dimensional arrays called embeddings. Each embedding represents semantic content as coordinates in a continuous vector space.

Look at the coordinate-plot to see how nearby points share semantic meaning.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Vector Distance in Embedding Space","caption":"Illustrative 2D coordinate-plot showing proximity between a query vector and item vectors.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Dimension 1","min":0,"max":5},"y":{"label":"Dimension 2","min":0,"max":5},"series":[{"label":"Stored Items","kind":"scatter","points":[{"x":1,"y":4,"label":"Item A"},{"x":4,"y":1,"label":"Item B"}]},{"label":"Query","kind":"scatter","points":[{"x":1.2,"y":3.8,"label":"Query Vector"}]}]}}
```

To retrieve results quickly without checking every stored record, these databases use approximate nearest neighbor indexing algorithms like hierarchical navigable small world graphs.

This structure partitions the space so queries skip unrelated clusters.

Once candidate vectors are identified, the system computes exact vector similarity metrics such as cosine similarity or Euclidean distance to rank the final matches.

runs.prompt: how are attention weights computed?
runs.title: Computing Attention Weights
runs.body:
Attention weights measure how much focus a query places on each key.

To compute them, we first take the dot product of the query vector $q$ with each key vector $k_j$, scaling by the inverse square root of the key dimension $\sqrt{d_k}$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Query and key dot products $q_i \\cdot k_j$","kind":"token-links","source":["key1","key2"],"target":["key1","key2"],"queries":[{"index":0,"weights":[0.8,0.2]}],"normalized":true}}
```

These raw scores pass through a softmax function to produce probabilities that sum to one. In the diagram above, the heaviest weight is $0.8$, showing high alignment for the first token.

$$\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

Scaling by $\sqrt{d_k}$ prevents gradients from vanishing when dimensionality grows large. This probability distribution then weights the value vectors to yield the final output representation.

runs.prompt: how are attention weights computed?
runs.title: Computing Attention Weights
runs.body:
Attention weights are computed using the dot product of queries $Q$ and keys $K$, scaled by the square root of the key dimension $d_k$.

Notice how the inner product measures the alignment between each query and key vector in the token-links diagram below.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Query-Key weights $w_1+w_2=1$","kind":"token-links","source":["key1","key2"],"target":["key1","key2"],"queries":[{"index":0,"weights":[0.8,0.2]}],"normalized":true}}
```

Mathematically, the scaled dot-product attention formula is defined as $\text{Softmax}(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}})V$.

This normalization prevents gradients from vanishing during backpropagation when dimensionality grows large.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy loss?
runs.title: Cross Entropy Loss
runs.body:
Cross entropy loss measures the dissimilarity between the predicted probability distribution and the true label distribution.

For a binary classification problem, the formula is defined as $L = -y \log(p) - (1-y) \log(1-p)$, where $y$ is the true label and $p$ is the predicted probability.

Observe how the loss curves diverge steeply as predictions become completely wrong in the plot below.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Cross-entropy depends on the true label","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Predicted positive probability","min":0.01,"max":0.99,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Loss","min":0,"max":5},"series":[{"label":"True class 1","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":4.605},{"x":0.1,"y":2.303},{"x":0.25,"y":1.386},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":0.288},{"x":0.9,"y":0.105},{"x":0.99,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"True class 0","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":0.01},{"x":0.1,"y":0.105},{"x":0.25,"y":0.288},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":1.386},{"x":0.9,"y":2.303},{"x":0.99,"y":4.605}]}],"annotations":[]}}
```

When the true label $y=1$, predicting a low probability $p$ incurs a very high loss that approaches infinity. Conversely, when $y=0$, predicting a high probability $p$ drives the second term up sharply.

Gradient descent uses this steep slope to heavily penalize confident misclassifications during training.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy loss?
runs.title: Cross Entropy Loss
runs.body:
Cross entropy loss measures the performance of a classification model whose output is a probability between $0$ and $1$.

The formula for a single binary observation is $L = -y \log(p) - (1-y) \log(1-p)$, where $y$ is the true label and $p$ is the predicted probability.

Notice how the penalty grows steeply as the prediction gets confidently wrong in the coordinate plot below.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Cross-entropy depends on the true label","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Predicted positive probability","min":0.01,"max":0.99,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Loss","min":0,"max":5},"series":[{"label":"True class 1","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":4.605},{"x":0.1,"y":2.303},{"x":0.25,"y":1.386},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":0.288},{"x":0.9,"y":0.105},{"x":0.99,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"True class 0","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":0.01},{"x":0.1,"y":0.105},{"x":0.25,"y":0.288},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":1.386},{"x":0.9,"y":2.303},{"x":0.99,"y":4.605}]}],"annotations":[]}}
```

When the true label $y = 1$, the loss function simplifies to $-\log(p)$, which penalizes confident wrong guesses with a very high penalty.

Conversely, when $y = 0$, the loss function simplifies to $-\log(1-p)$, penalizing probabilities close to $1$.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy loss?
runs.title: Cross Entropy Loss
runs.body:
When teaching a computer to pick categories, we need a way to measure how wrong its guesses are. Cross entropy loss is a scoring rule that penalizes confident wrong answers very harshly.

```rh-diagram

```

Imagine guessing a coin flip where the true outcome is heads. If the model assigns a low probability to heads, the cross entropy loss shoots up.

This steep penalty forces the model to adjust its weights quickly until it becomes more certain of the right category.

runs.body:
Cross entropy loss is a way to measure how wrong a computer model is when it guesses categories. If the model guesses a cat is very likely when it is actually a dog, the loss goes up.

Look at the values in the comparison diagram to see how predictions differ from reality. When the prediction matches the true label, the loss is close to zero.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy loss?
runs.title: Cross-Entropy Loss
runs.body:
When a model predicts a spam email with probability $p = 0.9$, but the true label is $y = 1$, we need a way to measure the penalty for being wrong.

Cross-entropy loss calculates this penalty using the formula $H(y, p) = -y \log p - (1 - y) \log (1 - p)$.

Observe how the penalty curves rise sharply toward infinity as predictions become confidently incorrect.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Cross-entropy depends on the true label","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Predicted positive probability","min":0.01,"max":0.99,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Loss","min":0,"max":5},"series":[{"label":"True class 1","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":4.605},{"x":0.1,"y":2.303},{"x":0.25,"y":1.386},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":0.288},{"x":0.9,"y":0.105},{"x":0.99,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"True class 0","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":0.01},{"x":0.1,"y":0.105},{"x":0.25,"y":0.288},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":1.386},{"x":0.9,"y":2.303},{"x":0.99,"y":4.605}]}],"annotations":[]}}
```

If the true label $y = 1$, the second term vanishes, leaving $-\log p$. If the model predicts $p = 0.01$, the loss surges to $4.605$, punishing confident mistakes heavily.

Conversely, when the prediction aligns with reality, $-\log(0.99)$ drops near zero.

When a classification model predicts a cat with 90 percent confidence but the true label is dog, it suffers a heavy penalty.

Cross-entropy loss measures the difference between two probability distributions: the true labels and the predicted outputs.

For a single binary decision, the penalty is defined as $L = -y \log(p) - (1-y) \log(1-p)$, where $y$ is the true class and $p$ is the predicted probability.

runs.prompt: what is batch normalization?
runs.title: Batch Normalization
runs.body:
Batch normalization stabilizes deep neural networks by normalizing layer inputs for every training batch. This reduces internal covariate shift, allowing higher learning rates and faster convergence.

Look at the transformation above to see how raw activations become normalized values.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Normalize layer inputs","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Mini-batch","items":["Raw activations $x_i$"]},"after":{"label":"Normalized","items":["Scaled values $y_i$"]},"operation":"Subtract mean, divide by std dev, then scale and shift"}}
```

For each mini-batch, the network computes the empirical mean and variance across the batch dimensions.

It then normalizes the activations and applies learnable parameters $\gamma$ and $\beta$ to preserve representation capacity.

runs.prompt: what is batch normalization?
runs.title: Batch Normalization
runs.body:
Batch normalization is a layer technique that stabilizes training in deep neural networks by recentering and rescaling layer inputs. Consider a mini-batch of activations passing through a network layer during training.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Batch normalization transformation","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Original activations","items":["Mean $\\mu_B$","Variance $\\sigma_B^2$"]},"after":{"label":"Normalized activations","items":["Mean $0$","Variance $1$"]},"operation":"Subtract $\\mu_B$, divide by $\\sqrt{\\sigma_B^2 + \\epsilon}$, then scale and shift"}}
```

For this mini-batch, the network computes the empirical mean $\mu_B$ and variance $\sigma_B^2$ across the batch dimension. Each activation is then normalized by subtracting $\mu_B$ and dividing by the standard deviation.

To preserve the representational power of the network, learnable parameters $\gamma$ and $\beta$ then scale and shift the normalized output.

This mechanism reduces internal covariate shift, allowing higher learning rates and faster convergence.

runs.prompt: how does dropout work?
runs.title: Dropout in Neural Networks
runs.body:
During training, dropout randomly deactivates hidden units to prevent overfitting. Look at the transformation diagram to see how units are masked during training and scaled during inference.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Dropout layer transformation","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Training phase","items":["All hidden units active","Random units dropped with rate $p$"]},"after":{"label":"Inference phase","items":["All units active","Weights scaled by keep rate $p$"]},"operation":"Apply Bernoulli mask during training and scale at test time"}}
```

This prevents complex co-adaptations among neurons. At test time, all units remain active while their outputs are scaled by the keep rate $p$.

runs.prompt: how does dropout work?
runs.title: Dropout Regularization
runs.body:
Dropout prevents neural networks from overfitting by randomly switching off a fraction of hidden units during each training step.

This forces the network to learn redundant representations rather than relying on any single pathway.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Dropout removes units during training","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Full hidden layer","items":["Unit 1","Unit 2","Unit 3"]},"after":{"label":"Thinned layer","items":["Unit 1","Dropped","Unit 3"]},"operation":"Drop units with probability 1 - p"}}
```

During training, each hidden unit is kept with a probability $p$ and dropped otherwise. At inference time, all units are active, but their outgoing weights are scaled by $p$ to match the expected activation magnitude.

runs.body:
In a transformer model, self-attention computes how much each token in a sequence relates to every other token. This mechanism compares queries against keys using dot products to measure relevance.

A softmax function then scales these scores into probabilities that sum to one.

These probability weights are multiplied by value vectors to produce a new context-aware representation for each token.

By doing this across multiple heads simultaneously, the network captures different types of semantic relationships.

runs.prompt: how does attention work in a transformer?
runs.title: Transformer Self-Attention Mechanism
runs.body:
Transformer self-attention computes how much each token in a sequence relates to every other token. Given an input sequence, every token projects into three vectors: a query, a key, and a value.

We calculate compatibility scores by taking the dot product of queries and keys.

Look at the matrix below to see how query and key scores mix into attention weights.


We scale these raw scores and apply a softmax function so that weights for each query row sum to one. Multiplying these normalized weights by the value vectors yields the final contextualized representation.

This mechanism lets models dynamically route information across distant parts of a sequence without recurrence.

runs.prompt: how are attention weights computed?
runs.title: Computing Attention Weights
runs.body:
Attention weights determine how much focus a model places on different parts of an input sequence when processing a specific token.

For instance, when translating the word kite, the model assigns distinct importance scores to every preceding word in the sentence.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Weights on words","kind":"token-links","source":["red","kite"],"target":["red","kite"],"queries":[{"index":1,"weights":[0.25,0.75]}],"normalized":true}}
```

These scores start as raw dot products between query vectors and key vectors, measuring the alignment between tokens. Looking at the diagram, the weights sum to one after passing through a softmax function.

Dividing by the square root of the key dimension scales these dot products to prevent vanishing gradients during training.

The resulting probabilities then multiply the value vectors to produce the final context representation.

runs.prompt: how are attention weights computed?
runs.title: Computing Attention Weights
runs.body:
Attention weights measure how much focus one token places on another in a sequence. To compute them, the model takes the dot product of a query vector and a key vector for each token pair.

Look for the assigned values in the diagram below, which show the distribution of attention across words.


These raw scores are then divided by the square root of the key dimension to stabilize gradients during training.

Finally, a softmax function is applied so that all weights are positive and sum to one across the target tokens.

runs.prompt: how does cross-validation detect overfitting?
runs.title: Cross-validation and overfitting
runs.body:
Overfitting happens when a model memorizes training data instead of learning general patterns, leading to poor predictions on new examples.

Cross-validation splits data into folds to train on some parts and test on others, revealing this gap.

Look at the high validation error compared to the tiny training error in to see how the model fails to generalize.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Error by model complexity","kind":"bar-chart","unit":"error","bars":[{"label":"Train error","value":0.05},{"label":"Validation error","value":0.35}]}}
```

When validation error diverges from training error, the model has overfit.

By averaging performance across multiple splits, cross-validation provides a reliable estimate of unseen data error.

runs.prompt: how does cross-validation detect overfitting?
runs.title: Cross-Validation and Overfitting
runs.body:
Overfitting occurs when a model learns the training data too well, capturing noise instead of the true underlying pattern. This causes high performance on training data but poor generalization to unseen data.

Observe the difference between training error and validation error in the chart below to spot this discrepancy.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Model Error by Complexity","kind":"bar-chart","unit":"error","bars":[{"label":"Train Error","value":0.05},{"label":"CV Error","value":0.35}]}}
```

Cross-validation detects this by splitting the dataset into multiple folds, training on some and testing on the left-out fold. When training error drops while validation error rises, the model is overfitting.

runs.prompt: How do attention scores turn into weights?
runs.title: From Attention Scores to Weights
runs.body:
When a transformer computes attention, it first calculates raw scores by taking the dot product of a query and key vectors.

To turn these raw scores into probabilities that sum to one, the model applies the softmax function across all target tokens.

Exponentiating the scores ensures all values are positive, while dividing by their sum normalizes the final distribution.

Larger raw scores receive exponentially higher weights, allowing the model to focus on the most relevant context.

runs.prompt: How do attention scores turn into weights?
runs.title: Turning attention scores into weights
runs.body:
When a transformer computes raw compatibility between tokens, it produces unscaled numbers called logits. These scores can be positive, negative, or arbitrarily large depending on vector dot products.

Look at the heavy weight connecting sat to cat in the diagram below, showing how the largest score dominates the distribution.


To turn these raw scores into valid probabilities, the model applies the softmax function across all target tokens.

Softmax exponentiates each score and divides by the sum of all exponentiated scores, forcing every resulting weight to be between zero and one.

These normalized weights sum to exactly one, allowing the model to take a weighted average of value vectors.

A transformer processes text by routing information through multiple independent pathways called attention heads.

Each head projects inputs into separate query, key, and value spaces to focus on different relational aspects simultaneously.

For example, in the sentence the cat sat on the mat, one head might link verbs to their subjects while another tracks spatial prepositions.

runs.prompt: Why does a transformer use more than one attention head?
runs.title: Why Transformers Use Multiple Attention Heads
runs.body:
A transformer processing the sentence the cat sat on the mat needs to track different relationships at the exact same time.

If it relied on a single set of attention weights, it would be forced to average out these diverse syntactic and semantic links into one blurry representation.

Notice how the two separate series in the chart assign completely different importance scores to the same six token positions for the word sat.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Attention weights by head and token","caption":"Both heads query sat. Head A puts the most weight on cat, and Head B puts the most on the first the.","kind":"bar-chart","variant":"grouped","categories":["1. the","2. cat","3. sat","4. on","5. the","6. mat"],"series":[{"label":"Head A","values":[0.052,0.65,0.192,0.059,0.02,0.027]},{"label":"Head B","values":[0.388,0.175,0.093,0.049,0.077,0.218]}]}}
```

To solve this limitation, multi-head attention splits the key, query, and value vectors into multiple subspaces known as attention heads.

runs.prompt: How does a transformer get a match score between words?
runs.title: Transformer Word Match Scores
runs.body:
Transformers compute match scores between words using vectors called queries and keys. For instance, when processing the word sat, its query vector multiplies every word's key vector to measure alignment.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Query-Key dot products and scaled scores","caption":"Compare the query for sat with each key, then divide by the square root of key width.","kind":"matrix","columns":["Dot product","Scaled score"],"rows":[{"heading":"the 1","cells":["-0.539","-0.381"]},{"heading":"cat 2","cells":["3.034","2.145"]},{"heading":"sat 3","cells":["1.306","0.923"]}]}}
```

These raw products grow large as vector dimensions increase, pushing softmax functions into regions with tiny gradients. Dividing by the square root of the dimension scales the variance back, stabilizing training.

This resulting scaled score determines how much focus one word places on another.

runs.prompt: How does a transformer get a match score between words?
runs.title: Transformer Word Match Scores
runs.body:
Transformers compute match scores between words using vector dot products. Take the query vector $q$ for a word and compare it against key vectors $k$ for all other words.

Multiplying these vectors yields a raw dot product that measures alignment. Look at the matrix values in to see how raw products become scaled scores.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Attention dot products and scaled scores","caption":"Compare the query for sat with each key, then divide by the square root of the shown key width.","kind":"matrix","layout":"teaching","columns":["Dot product","Scaled score"],"rows":[{"id":"k1","heading":"the 1","cells":["-0.539","-0.381"]},{"id":"k2","heading":"cat 2","cells":["3.034","2.145"]},{"id":"k3","heading":"sat 3","cells":["1.306","0.923"]}]}}
```

Because large vector dimensions push dot products to extreme values, models divide each result by the square root of the key dimension $d_k$. This scaling stabilizes gradients during training.

The resulting scaled dot products form the attention weights after a softmax operation.

runs.prompt: How does a transformer mix the word values after it has attention weights?
runs.title: Weighted Value Mixing in Attention
runs.body:
Once attention weights are calculated, each value vector is multiplied by its scalar weight. This scales the importance of each word representation before combination.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Weighted values for sat","kind":"block-stack","orientation":"horizontal","blocks":[{"id":"a","label":"the 0.052","dims":"256"},{"id":"b","label":"cat 0.65","dims":"256"},{"id":"c","label":"sat 0.192","dims":"256"}]}}
```

Finally, all these scaled vectors are summed together to form a single combined context vector. This resulting vector captures the contextual meaning for the target token.

runs.prompt: How does a transformer mix the word values after it has attention weights?
runs.title: Mixing word values with attention weights
runs.body:
Once attention scores are turned into probabilities that sum to $1$, the model mixes token representations by computing a weighted sum.

Each value vector, representing the content of a word, is multiplied by its corresponding attention weight. Look at the multiplier strips in the diagram to see how each vector scales before the final combination.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Weighted values for tokens","kind":"block-stack","orientation":"horizontal","blocks":[{"id":"a","label":"token 0.05","dims":"256","diagram":{"kind":"tensor","tensor":{"rows":1,"columns":2,"dimensions":"256","values":[0.2,1.4]}}},{"id":"b","label":"token 0.65","dims":"256","diagram":{"kind":"tensor","tensor":{"rows":1,"columns":2,"dimensions":"256","values":[0.3,1]}}},{"id":"c","label":"token 0.30","dims":"256","diagram":{"kind":"tensor","tensor":{"rows":1,"columns":2,"dimensions":"256","values":[0.7,1.4]}}}]}}
```

After scaling every vector by its attention probability, the transformer adds all the resulting vectors together into a single output vector.

This step blends context from all relevant words into the current token's representation.

runs.prompt: How does a transformer get query, key and value vectors from one token?
runs.title: Query, Key, and Value Projections
runs.body:
A transformer takes each input token and generates three distinct vectors for attention: a query, a key, and a value.

These vectors allow the model to search for relevant context across the sequence during self-attention.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"One token, three attention projections","caption":"The input embedding multiplies three distinct weight matrices to form query, key, and value vectors.","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Input Token","items":[{"tensor":{"rows":1,"columns":4,"dimensions":"1 × 512","name":"Embedding","values":[1.109,-0.516,0.72,1.4],"role":"input"}}]},"after":{"label":"Projected Vectors","items":[{"tensor":{"rows":1,"columns":2,"dimensions":"1 × 256","name":"Query","values":[1.829,-0.516],"role":"output"}},{"tensor":{"rows":1,"columns":2,"dimensions":"1 × 256","name":"Key","values":[1.109,1.4],"role":"output"}},{"tensor":{"rows":1,"columns":2,"dimensions":"1 × 256","name":"Value","values":[0.72,1.4],"role":"output"}}]},"operation":"Multiply by learned weight matrices $W_Q$, $W_K$, and $W_V$","links":[{"from":0,"to":0},{"from":0,"to":1},{"from":0,"to":2}]}}
```

The transformation begins with the token's combined embedding vector $x$. This vector multiplies three separately learned weight matrices $W_Q$, $W_K$, and $W_V$.

Each matrix projects the input into a specialized subspace, creating the query, key, and value representations.

runs.prompt: How does a transformer get query, key and value vectors from one token?
runs.title: Query, Key, and Value Projections
runs.body:
When a transformer processes a sequence, each input token starts as a combined embedding vector that captures its semantic meaning and position.

To compute self-attention, the model multiplies this single input vector by three separate, learned weight matrices to produce three new vectors: the query, the key, and the value.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"One token, three attention projections","caption":"One token embedding transforms into three distinct vectors via learned matrices.","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Input token","items":[{"tensor":{"rows":1,"columns":4,"dimensions":"1 x 512","name":"Embedding","values":[1.109,-0.516,0.72,1.4],"role":"input"}}]},"after":{"label":"Projected vectors","items":[{"tensor":{"rows":1,"columns":2,"dimensions":"1 x 256","name":"Query","values":[1.829,-0.516],"role":"output"}},{"tensor":{"rows":1,"columns":2,"dimensions":"1 x 256","name":"Key","values":[1.109,1.4],"role":"output"}},{"tensor":{"rows":1,"columns":2,"dimensions":"1 x 256","name":"Value","values":[0.72,1.4],"role":"output"}}]},"operation":"Multiply by learned weight matrices","links":[{"from":0,"to":0},{"from":0,"to":1},{"from":0,"to":2}]}}
```

The query vector represents what the token is currently looking for in other tokens.

The key vector acts as a label describing what kind of information the token holds, and the value vector contains the actual content to be shared.

By taking the dot product of queries and keys, the model determines how much attention to pay to each part of the sequence.

runs.prompt: how does cross-validation detect overfitting?
runs.title: Cross-Validation and Overfitting Detection
runs.body:
Cross-validation detects overfitting by partitioning data into $k$ folds to measure generalization error. When a model fits training data too closely, its parameters capture noise rather than true underlying patterns.

Looking at the chart, notice the gap between the low training error and the high validation error.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Error by model complexity","caption":"Validation error rises as training error drops.","kind":"bar-chart","unit":"error","bars":[{"label":"Train Error","value":0.05},{"label":"Valid Error","value":0.35}]}}
```

This divergence reveals that the complex hypothesis fails to perform on unseen validation folds. Regularization and simpler models help bridge this generalization gap.

runs.prompt: how does cross-validation detect overfitting?
runs.title: Cross-Validation and Overfitting
runs.body:
Cross-validation detects overfitting by partitioning the dataset into $k$ folds, training the model on $k-1$ folds, and testing its performance on the remaining held-out fold.

This rotation repeats until every fold has served as the validation set, yielding an aggregate performance estimate on unseen data.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Training versus validation error","caption":"Illustrative values showing validation error increasing as complexity grows past the optimum.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Model complexity","min":1,"max":5},"y":{"label":"Error rate","min":0,"max":0.5},"series":[{"label":"Training error","kind":"line","points":[{"x":1,"y":0.35},{"x":2,"y":0.25},{"x":3,"y":0.15},{"x":4,"y":0.08},{"x":5,"y":0.02}]},{"label":"Validation error","kind":"line","points":[{"x":1,"y":0.38},{"x":2,"y":0.27},{"x":3,"y":0.2},{"x":4,"y":0.28},{"x":5,"y":0.42}]}],"annotations":[{"kind":"point","label":"Overfitting point","x":5,"y":0.42}]}}
```

When a model fits the training data too closely, training error drops while validation error increases.

The divergence between these two curves signals that the model has memorized noise rather than learning generalizable patterns.

In practice, $k$ is commonly set to 5 or 10 to balance computational cost and variance.

runs.title: Softmax conversion of attention scores
runs.body:
The attention mechanism first computes a raw score $s_i$ for each token, often as a dot‑product of query and key vectors.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Attention weights from scores","caption":"Apply softmax $w_i=\\exp(s_i)/\\sum_j\\exp(s_j)$ to the six scores. The shown weights sum to one.","kind":"token-links","source":["the","cat","sat","on","the","mat"],"target":["the","cat","sat","on","the","mat"],"queries":[{"index":2,"weights":[0.052,0.65,0.192,0.059,0.02,0.027]}],"normalized":true}}
```

Softmax turns these scores into a probability distribution. Each weight $w_i$ is the exponential of its score divided by the sum of all exponentials, guaranteeing $\sum_i w_i=1$.

The resulting weights indicate how much each token contributes to the context vector; larger scores produce exponentially larger weights, while very low scores receive near‑zero weight.

runs.prompt: How do attention scores turn into weights?
runs.title: Converting Attention Scores to Weights
runs.body:
Attention scores $s_j = q \cdot k_j$ measure raw alignment between a query and each key. These real-valued scores can be negative or arbitrarily large.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Softmax over scores","caption":"Compute $a_j=\\exp(s_j)/\\sum_i\\exp(s_i)$ to ensure weights sum to one.","kind":"token-links","source":["key1","key2"],"target":["key1","key2"],"queries":[{"index":0,"weights":[0.73,0.27]}],"normalized":true}}
```

To turn them into a probability distribution, the softmax function exponentiates each score and divides by the sum across all keys. The resulting weights $a_j$ are strictly positive and sum to one.

runs.title: Causal Masking in a Transformer Decoder
runs.body:
The decoder must not use information from future tokens when predicting the current one. It does this by adding a causal mask to the attention scores.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"kind":"heatmap","title":"Causal mask before softmax","caption":"Gray cells are -∞ (blocked) for j>i, zeros otherwise. Shows which key positions each query can attend to.","rowLabel":"Query position","columnLabel":"Key position","columns":["1","2","3","4","5","6"],"rows":[{"label":"1","cells":[0,null,null,null,null,null]},{"label":"2","cells":[0,0,null,null,null,null]},{"label":"3","cells":[0,0,0,null,null,null]},{"label":"4","cells":[0,0,0,0,null,null]},{"label":"5","cells":[0,0,0,0,0,null]},{"label":"6","cells":[0,0,0,0,0,0]}],"range":{"min":-1,"max":0}}}
```

The mask sets any score where the key index j exceeds the query index i to $-\infty$, forcing the softmax to assign zero probability. Only the diagonal and lower‑triangular entries remain.

After adding the mask, the softmax normalises each row over the allowed keys, so the attention distribution for query i sums to 1 and contains no contribution from later positions.

This mechanism guarantees strict left‑to‑right generation, preventing the model from “looking ahead.”

runs.title: Causal Masking in the Transformer Decoder
runs.body:
The transformer decoder prevents illegal attention to future tokens by applying an additive causal mask $M$ to the scaled dot-product attention scores before computing the softmax function.

For a sequence length $n$, the mask matrix $M_{ij}$ is defined as $0$ when $j \le i$ and $-\infty$ when $j > i$, ensuring that query position $i$ cannot attend to key position $j$ beyond the current step.

Look at the heatmap above to see how upper triangular entries are blocked with negative infinity while lower entries remain unmasked.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Causal masking before softmax","caption":"Across six positions, add $M_{ij}=-\\infty$ when $j>i$ and $0$ otherwise. Gray cells show the blocked scores.","kind":"flow","nodes":[{"id":"n1","label":"the 1","role":"process"},{"id":"n2","label":"cat 2","role":"process"},{"id":"n3","label":"sat 3","role":"process"},{"id":"n4","label":"on 4","role":"process"},{"id":"n5","label":"the 5","role":"process"},{"id":"n6","label":"mat 6","role":"outcome"}],"edges":[{"from":"n1","to":"n2"},{"from":"n2","to":"n3"},{"from":"n3","to":"n4"},{"from":"n4","to":"n5"},{"from":"n5","to":"n6"}]}}
```

In practice, this autoregressive constraint preserves the causal ordering required for generative language modeling during both training and inference phases.

runs.prompt: How does the decoder use the encoder's words while writing the next word?
runs.title: Cross-Attention in Decoders
runs.body:
Cross-attention lets the decoder fetch relevant context from the encoder's output sequence during text generation.

The query vector $q$ comes from the current decoder state, while keys $k$ and values $v$ come from the encoder hidden states.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Decoder query over encoder keys","caption":"The shown query component scores encoder keys as $qk_j^\\top/\\root{2}$. Softmax weights the encoder values.","kind":"token-links","source":["the","cat","sat"],"target":["the","cat","sat","on","the","mat"],"queries":[{"index":2,"weights":[0.173,0.211,0.229,0.15,0.14,0.097]}],"normalized":true}}
```

The dot product $qk^\top$ computes how much each encoder word matters, scaled by $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}$.

Applying softmax yields weights that sum to one, combining the encoder values into a single context vector for the decoder.

runs.prompt: How does the decoder use the encoder's words while writing the next word?
runs.title: Decoder Cross-Attention Over Encoder Words
runs.body:
Cross-attention connects the decoder to the encoder outputs during text generation. Each decoder layer computes queries $Q$ from its own prior steps, while keys $K$ and values $V$ come from the final encoder states.

Look for the probability weights assigned from the decoder query word sat to each encoder word in the diagram below.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Decoder query over encoder keys","caption":"The query component scores encoder keys as $qk_j^\\top/\\sqrt{2}$. Softmax across all six keys weights the encoder values.","kind":"token-links","source":["the","cat","sat"],"target":["the","cat","sat","on","the","mat"],"queries":[{"index":2,"weights":[0.173,0.211,0.229,0.15,0.14,0.097]}],"normalized":true}}
```

Dot products $QK^\top$ measure alignment between the current generation state and all source positions. Scaling by $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}$ stabilizes gradients before softmax turns these scores into attention weights.

The resulting weights multiply the value vectors to form a context vector that guides the next token prediction.

runs.prompt: Why does a transformer use more than one attention head?
runs.title: Multi-Head Attention in Transformers
runs.body:
Transformers use multi-head attention to project queries, keys, and values into different representation subspaces simultaneously.

Given $H$ heads, the input vector dimension $d_{\text{model}}$ is split across the heads so each operates on a subspace of dimension $d_k = d_{\text{model}} / H$.

Each head learns independent linear projections $W_i^Q, W_i^K, W_i^V$, allowing the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions.

Look at how the attention weights shift across the different token positions in the chart below.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Attention weights by head and token","caption":"Both heads query sat. Head A puts the most weight on cat, and Head B puts the most on the first the.","kind":"bar-chart","variant":"grouped","categories":["1. the","2. cat","3. sat","4. on","5. the","6. mat"],"series":[{"label":"Head A","values":[0.052,0.65,0.192,0.059,0.02,0.027]},{"label":"Head B","values":[0.388,0.175,0.093,0.049,0.077,0.218]}]}}
```

Without multiple heads, a single attention mechanism averages out these diverse relational roles into one blended distribution.

runs.prompt: Why does a transformer use more than one attention head?
runs.title: Multi-Head Attention in Transformers
runs.body:
Transformers use multi-head attention to project queries, keys, and values into different representation subspaces simultaneously.

Instead of performing a single attention function, the model splits the hidden dimension $d_{\text{model}}$ into $h$ distinct heads, running attention in parallel.

