Head A puts the most weight on cat, and Head B puts the most on the first the.","kind":"bar-chart","variant":"grouped","categories":["1. the","2. cat","3. sat","4. on","5. the","6. mat"],"series":[{"label":"Head A","values":[0.052,0.65,0.192,0.059,0.02,0.027]},{"label":"Head B","values":[0.388,0.175,0.093,0.049,0.077,0.218]}]}}

Each head can focus on different positions and relationships, such as syntactic links or semantic roles.

The outputs are concatenated and linearly transformed back to the expected dimension, allowing the network to capture varied features at once.

runs.prompt: How does a transformer get a match score between words?
runs.title: Transformer word match scores
runs.body:
Transformers compute match scores by taking the dot product of a query vector and a key vector for every token pair.

This raw product grows large in high dimensions, so it is scaled down by dividing by the square root of the key dimension $\sqrt{d_k}$.

```rh-diagram

```

The resulting values form the input to the softmax function, which turns them into positive weights summing to one.

These weights determine how much focus each token places on all other context tokens during self-attention.

runs.prompt: How does a transformer get a match score between words?
runs.title: Transformer Word Match Scores
runs.body:
Transformers compute word matches using the dot product of query and key vectors. For a query $q$ and key $k_j$, the raw score is $q \cdot k_j$. Look at the matrix below to see the dot products and their scaled values.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Scaled dot-product scores for sat","caption":"Use $s_j=(q\\cdot k_j)/\\sqrt{d_k}$ for each key, with $d_k=2$ shown out of 256 entries.","kind":"matrix","layout":"teaching","columns":["Dot product","Scaled score"],"rows":[{"id":"k1","heading":"the 1","cells":["-0.539","-0.381"]},{"id":"k2","heading":"cat 2","cells":["3.034","2.145"]},{"id":"k3","heading":"sat 3","cells":["1.306","0.923"]}]}}
```

To stabilize training, this raw dot product is scaled by dividing by the square root of the key dimension $\sqrt{d_k}$.

When dimensions grow large, unscaled dot products grow too wide and push softmax gradients near zero. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ keeps the variance equal to one.

runs.prompt: How does a transformer mix the word values after it has attention weights?
runs.title: Mixing Word Values with Attention Weights
runs.body:
Once attention weights are computed, the transformer mixes value vectors by taking their weighted sum. Each weight $a_j$ scales its corresponding value vector $v_j$ across all dimensions.

Look for the scaled vectors in the diagram below to see how individual contributions are sized.

```rh-diagram

```

The final mixed vector is produced by summing these scaled items as $z = \sum_j a_j v_j$. This operation combines context from all attended tokens into a single representation for the target position.

runs.prompt: How does a transformer mix the word values after it has attention weights?
runs.title: Mixing Word Values With Attention Weights
runs.body:
Once attention weights are computed, the model forms the output vector by calculating a weighted sum of all value vectors.

Look at the block stack diagram to see how each word value is multiplied by its scalar weight before summation.

The operation is expressed as $z = \sum_j a_j v_j$, where $a_j$ is the attention weight and $v_j$ is the value vector.

In practice, this weighted combination allows the target token to gather relevant context from every other position in the sequence.

Each head performs this mixing independently across its subspaces before concatenating and projecting the results.

runs.prompt: what is maximum likelihood estimation?
runs.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation
runs.body:
Maximum likelihood estimation finds parameter values that maximize the likelihood function for observed data.

Given a statistical model with parameters $\theta$ and independent observations $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$, the joint probability density function defines the likelihood $L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i \mid \theta)$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Likelihood function for parameter $\\theta$","caption":"The maximum likelihood estimate maximizes the probability of observing the given data.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Parameter $\\theta$","min":0,"max":10},"y":{"label":"Log-Likelihood $L(\\theta)$","min":-20,"max":0},"series":[{"label":"$L(\\theta)$","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":-18},{"x":2,"y":-10},{"x":4,"y":-4},{"x":5,"y":-2,"label":"MLE"},{"x":6,"y":-3},{"x":8,"y":-10},{"x":10,"y":-19}]}]}}
```

In practice, we maximize the log-likelihood function $\ln L(\theta)$ to convert products into sums, simplifying differentiation.

Setting the derivative to zero yields the score equation $\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \ln L(\theta) = 0$, whose solution gives the estimator $\hat{\theta}$.

runs.prompt: what is maximum likelihood estimation?
runs.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation
runs.body:
Maximum likelihood estimation is a method of estimating the parameters of a probability distribution by maximizing a likelihood function so that the observed data is most probable.

Given independent and identically distributed data $x_1, x_2, ..., x_n$ with probability density function $f(x|\theta)$, the joint likelihood function is defined as $L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i|\theta)$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Likelihood function for parameter $\\theta$","caption":"The maximum likelihood estimate $\\hat{\\theta}$ maximizes the likelihood $L(\\theta|x)$ of the observed data.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Parameter $\\theta$","min":0,"max":10},"y":{"label":"Likelihood $L(\\theta)$","min":0,"max":25},"series":[{"label":"$L(\\theta)$","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0},{"x":2,"y":8},{"x":4,"y":18},{"x":5,"y":20,"label":"$\\hat{\\theta}$"},{"x":6,"y":18},{"x":8,"y":8},{"x":10,"y":0}]}]}}
```

In practice, we maximize the natural logarithm of the likelihood function, known as the log-likelihood $\ln L(\theta)$, to turn products into simpler sums.

The maximum likelihood estimate $\hat{\theta}$ is found by taking the derivative of the log-likelihood with respect to $\theta$ and setting it to zero.

runs.body:
Overfitting happens when a model learns the training data too well, capturing noise instead of the underlying pattern. This results in poor generalization to unseen data.

Look for the held-out point and the curves in the plot below to see how an overfit model deviates from general trends.


As $\alpha$ increases, branches that provide insufficient predictive gains are systematically snipped off, shrinking the tree.

Both measures start at zero when the node is pure ($p=0$ or $p=1$) and reach a maximum when the classes are evenly split.

Notice the curves in the plot where Gini peaks at $0.5$ and entropy peaks at $1.0$.

Gini impurity is $2p(1-p)$ and entropy is $-p\\log_2 p-(1-p)\\log_2(1-p)$.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Class fraction p","min":0,"max":1},"y":{"label":"Impurity score","min":0,"max":1},"series":[{"label":"Gini impurity","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0},{"x":0.2,"y":0.32},{"x":0.4,"y":0.48},{"x":0.5,"y":0.5,"label":"Gini peak"},{"x":0.6,"y":0.48},{"x":0.8,"y":0.32},{"x":1,"y":0}]},{"label":"Entropy (bits)","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0},{"x":0.2,"y":0.722},{"x":0.4,"y":0.971},{"x":0.5,"y":1,"label":"Entropy peak"},{"x":0.6,"y":0.971},{"x":0.8,"y":0.722},{"x":1,"y":0}]}]}}

Each leaf predicts the mean target value of the samples inside it, creating a piecewise constant step function approximation.

runs.prompt: how do I compute the Gini impurity on both sides of a split and the information gain?
runs.title: Computing Gini Impurity and Information Gain
runs.body:
To measure how mixed a node is, we use Gini impurity, defined as $1 - \sum p_i^2$ for class probabilities $p_i$.

Suppose a parent node splits into two equal child nodes, where the left child has four samples of class zero and the right child has one of class zero and three of class one.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Gini Impurity after split","caption":"Worked example combining child Ginis in proportion to their sizes.","kind":"matrix","columns":["Class 0","Class 1","Gini","Weight"],"rows":[{"heading":"Left","cells":["4","0","0","0.5"]},{"heading":"Right","cells":["1","3","0.375","0.5"]},{"heading":"After","cells":["—","—","0.1875","1"]}]}}
```

For the left child, the Gini impurity is zero because all items belong to class zero. For the right child, the Gini impurity is $1 - (1/4)^2 - (3/4)^2 = 0.375$.

To find the combined impurity after the split, we take the weighted average of the two child nodes. Since each child gets half the samples, the weighted impurity is $0.5 \times 0 + 0.5 \times 0.375 = 0.1875$.

runs.prompt: how do I compute the Gini impurity on both sides of a split and the information gain?
runs.title: Gini Impurity and Information Gain
runs.body:
Computing Gini impurity measures how often a randomly chosen element would be incorrectly labeled. For a node, the impurity is $1 - \sum p_i^2$, where $p_i$ is the probability of class $i$.

Consider a root node split into two children with equal weights of $0.5$.

Look for the child Ginis and their weighted combination in the matrix table above.

The left child has four instances of class zero and zero of class one, giving a Gini of zero. The right child has one instance of class zero and three of class one, yielding a Gini of $1 - ((1/4)^2 + (3/4)^2) = 0.375$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Gini after the root split","caption":"Worked example. Combine the child Ginis in proportion to their sizes.","kind":"matrix","columns":["Class 0","Class 1","Gini","Weight"],"rows":[{"heading":"Left","cells":["4","0","0","0.5"]},{"heading":"Right","cells":["1","3","0.375","0.5"]},{"heading":"After","cells":["—","—","0.1875","1"]}]}}
```

Subtracting this from the parent impurity yields the total gain achieved by the split.

runs.title: Reading a Delivery Time Box Plot
runs.body:
When you wait for packages, a box plot helps you see how long deliveries take without getting lost in every single number.

Think of it as a compact summary showing the fastest times, the slowest normal times, and where most orders land.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Delivery times in minutes","caption":"The box spans from the first quartile 16 to the third quartile 24.5, with median 20 and an outlier at 60.","kind":"box-plot","x":{"label":"Minutes","min":0,"max":65,"unit":"min"},"boxes":[{"label":"Deliveries","whiskerLow":12,"q1":16,"median":20,"q3":24.5,"whiskerHigh":25,"fences":{"lower":3.25,"upper":37.25},"outliers":[{"label":"Late order","value":60}]}]}}
```

The box in the middle covers the middle half of all your delivery times, stretching from the lower quarter to the upper quarter.

A bold line inside that box shows the exact middle time where half the orders were faster and half were slower. The whiskers reach out to the lowest and highest normal delivery times.

Any delivery that takes way longer than the rest appears far off to the right as an isolated point called an outlier.

runs.title: Finding unusual response times with IQR
runs.body:
When measuring how long a computer takes to reply, most values group close together while occasional spikes happen.

To spot these unusual delays reliably, statisticians use the interquartile range, which measures the span of the middle half of your data.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Response times with IQR fence and outlier","caption":"IQR = 104 - 90 = 14. Upper fence = 104 + 1.5 * 14 = 125. The 300 ms value is an outlier.","kind":"box-plot","x":{"label":"Time (ms)","min":60,"max":320,"unit":"ms"},"boxes":[{"label":"Response times","whiskerLow":80,"q1":90,"median":95,"q3":104,"whiskerHigh":110,"fences":{"lower":69,"upper":125},"outliers":[{"label":"Slow response","value":300}]}]}}
```

For your nine response times, the middle values give an interquartile range of fourteen milliseconds.

Multiplying this spread by one point five and adding it to the upper quartile creates an upper fence at one hundred twenty-five milliseconds.

Any data point sitting beyond this fence is marked separately as an outlier.

runs.title: Spotting Outliers with the 1.5 x IQR Rule
runs.body:
When a website takes too long to load, a single huge delay can throw off our view of normal speed. A box plot helps us see the typical spread of these response times without letting extreme spikes hide the pattern.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Response times with outlier","caption":"IQR is 16, fences are 63.5 and 127.5, and 300 ms is an outlier.","kind":"box-plot","x":{"label":"ms","min":50,"max":320,"unit":"ms"},"boxes":[{"label":"Response times","whiskerLow":80,"q1":87.5,"median":95,"q3":103.5,"whiskerHigh":110,"fences":{"lower":63.5,"upper":127.5},"outliers":[{"label":"Lag spike","value":300}]}]}}
```

The 1.5 x IQR rule finds extreme values by measuring the middle half of our data, known as the interquartile range. Any point sitting past a safety boundary, called a fence, gets marked separately as an unusual outlier.

For our response times, the middle half spans from 87.5 to 103.5 ms, giving a spread of 16 ms. Multiplying that spread by 1.5 and stretching it past the edges sets our upper fence at 127.5 ms.

runs.prompt: what is gini impurity
runs.title: Gini Impurity Formula and Curve
runs.body:
Gini impurity measures how often a randomly chosen element from a set would be incorrectly labeled if it were randomly labeled according to the distribution of labels in the subset.

For a binary classification task with probability $p$ of the positive class, the formula is $I_G(p) = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{J} p_i^2 = 2p(1-p)$.

Observe how the curve peaks at $p = 0.5$ where uncertainty is maximal, and drops to zero at the boundaries where the node is pure.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Gini Impurity for a Binary Split","caption":"Impurity peaks at $p=0.5$ and falls to zero at pure nodes.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Probability $p$","min":0,"max":1},"y":{"label":"Gini Impurity $I_G(p)$","min":0,"max":0.5},"series":[{"label":"$1 - p^2 - (1-p)^2$","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0},{"x":0.2,"y":0.32},{"x":0.4,"y":0.48},{"x":0.5,"y":0.5,"label":"(0.5, 0.5)"},{"x":0.6,"y":0.48},{"x":0.8,"y":0.32},{"x":1,"y":0}]}]}}
```

In decision trees, the splitting criterion computes the weighted sum of child impurities to maximize information gain at each node.

For a node with $K$ classes, the exact formula is $I_G(p) = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{K} p_i^2$, where $p_i$ is the probability of a randomly chosen item belonging to class $i$.

Notice how the curve peaks when classes are evenly split and drops to zero when pure.

runs.prompt: what does softmax do?
runs.title: Softmax Function Transformation
runs.body:
The softmax function maps a vector of arbitrary real-valued scores, called logits, into a probability distribution.

Given a vector $z$, each element is exponentiated to ensure positivity and divided by the sum of all exponentiated values.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Softmax layer transformation","caption":"Raw logit scores are exponentiated and normalized by the sum to form probabilities.","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Logits","items":["z_1 = 2.0","z_2 = 1.0","z_3 = 0.1"]},"after":{"label":"Probabilities","items":["p_1 = 0.659","p_2 = 0.242","p_3 = 0.099"]},"operation":"Apply softmax function"}}
```

The exact formula is $\sigma(z)_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j} e^{z_j}}$. This ensures that all output probabilities lie in the open interval $(0, 1)$ and sum exactly to $1$.

A primary limitation in practice is numerical overflow when logits are very large positive numbers. This is standardly mitigated by subtracting the maximum logit value from all elements before exponentiation.

runs.body:
The softmax function transforms a vector of raw, unconstrained real-valued scores into a discrete probability distribution.

Given a vector $z$, each component is exponentiated to ensure non-negativity and amplified relative differences, then normalized by the sum of all exponentiated components.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Converting raw scores to probabilities","caption":"The softmax function exponentiates raw logits and divides by their sum to yield a probability distribution.","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Raw scores (logits)","items":["2.0","1.0","0.1"]},"after":{"label":"Probabilities","items":["0.659","0.242","0.099"]},"operation":"Apply softmax formula $\\sigma(z)_i = \\frac{e^{z_i}}{\\sum_{j} e^{z_j}}$"}}
```

This normalization guarantees that the resulting output values lie strictly between $0$ and $1$ and sum up to exactly $1$.

In practice, its main failure mode is numerical overflow when logits are very large, which is standardly resolved by subtracting the maximum logit before exponentiation.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy
runs.title: Cross-Entropy Loss Function
runs.body:
Cross-entropy measures the difference between two probability distributions, typically the true labels and predicted probabilities. The binary cross-entropy loss formula is $H(y, p) = -y \log p - (1-y) \log (1-p)$.

Observe the plotted curve to see how penalty grows rapidly as prediction error increases.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Cross-entropy loss by predicted probability","caption":"Loss increases toward infinity as predicted probability diverges from the true class.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Predicted probability $p$","min":0.01,"max":0.99},"y":{"label":"Loss","min":0,"max":5},"series":[{"label":"True class 1 ($y=1$)","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":4.605},{"x":0.1,"y":2.303},{"x":0.25,"y":1.386},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":0.288},{"x":0.9,"y":0.105},{"x":0.99,"y":0.01}]}]}}
```

When the true label $y = 1$, the second term vanishes and the penalty is $-\log p$. If the model predicts $p = 0.01$, the loss surges to $4.605$, heavily penalizing confident mistakes.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy
runs.title: Cross-Entropy Formula and Properties
runs.body:
Cross-entropy measures the difference between two probability distributions, typically a true distribution $p$ and an estimated distribution $q$.

For discrete distributions, the formula is defined as $H(p, q) = -", \text{sum}_x p(x) \log q(x)$.

Notice how the penalty rises steeply as predictions diverge from the true labels in the plot.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Cross-entropy loss curves","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Predicted positive probability","min":0.01,"max":0.99,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Loss","min":0,"max":5},"series":[{"label":"True class 1","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":4.605},{"x":0.1,"y":2.303},{"x":0.25,"y":1.386},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":0.288},{"x":0.9,"y":0.105},{"x":0.99,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"True class 0","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":0.01},{"x":0.1,"y":0.105},{"x":0.25,"y":0.288},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":1.386},{"x":0.9,"y":2.303},{"x":0.99,"y":4.605}]}],"annotations":[]}}
```

In classification tasks, binary cross-entropy simplifies to $-\left(y \log \hat{y} + (1-y) \log (1-\hat{y})\right)$.

This formulation penalizes confident, incorrect predictions heavily because the logarithm approaches negative infinity.

runs.prompt: what is gradient descent?
runs.title: Gradient Descent Optimization
runs.body:
Gradient descent minimizes a differentiable loss function $L(w)$ by iteratively updating parameters along the negative gradient vector $-\nabla L(w)$.

Each parameter update depends on the learning rate $\alpha$, scaling step sizes via $w_{t+1} = w_t - \alpha \nabla L(w_t)$.

Observe the plotted vector steps in as parameters descend toward the local minimum.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Descent path on quadratic loss","caption":"Illustrative steps moving towards the minimum.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Weight $w_1$","min":-3,"max":3},"y":{"label":"Weight $w_2$","min":-3,"max":3},"series":[{"label":"Loss contour","kind":"line","closed":true,"samples":{"radius":2,"count":16}}],"annotations":[{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 1","from":{"x":-1.5,"y":1.1},"to":{"x":-0.9,"y":0.7}}]}}
```

Choosing an optimal learning rate prevents slow convergence or numerical divergence, ensuring stable parameter optimization.

runs.prompt: what is gradient descent?
runs.title: Gradient Descent Optimization
runs.body:
Gradient descent minimizes a scalar loss function $L(w)$ by iteratively updating parameters along the negative gradient vector.

The exact update rule is defined as $w_{t+1} = w_t - \eta \nabla L(w_t)$, where $\eta > 0$ represents the learning rate scalar.

Observe how successive steps cross decreasing loss contours until reaching the minimum at the origin.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"A descent path on a quadratic loss","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Weight 1","min":-3,"max":3,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Weight 2","min":-3,"max":3},"series":[{"label":"Outer loss contour","kind":"line","closed":true,"samples":{"radius":2,"count":16}},{"label":"Inner loss contour","kind":"line","closed":true,"samples":{"radius":1,"count":16}}],"annotations":[{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 1","from":{"x":-1.5,"y":1.1},"to":{"x":-0.9,"y":0.7}},{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 2","from":{"x":-0.9,"y":0.7},"to":{"x":-0.4,"y":0.3}},{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 3","from":{"x":-0.4,"y":0.3},"to":{"x":0,"y":0}}]}}
```

Choosing the step size $\eta$ requires care because an excessive rate causes divergence away from the minimum. Conversely, a minuscule rate leads to extremely slow convergence before reaching the stopping threshold.

runs.prompt: what is a learning rate schedule?
runs.title: Learning Rate Schedules
runs.body:
A learning rate schedule dynamically alters the step size $\eta$ during training to balance rapid initial convergence with stable fine-tuning.

Keeping $\eta$ constant often causes optimization to oscillate around the minimum without settling.

Observe how both step decay and exponential decay reduce $\eta$ over epochs in the plot below.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Learning-rate schedules share an epoch axis","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Epoch","min":0,"max":6,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Learning rate","min":0.001,"max":0.1,"scale":"log"},"series":[{"label":"Step decay","kind":"step","points":[{"x":0,"y":0.1},{"x":2,"y":0.03},{"x":4,"y":0.01},{"x":6,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"Exponential decay","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0.1},{"x":1,"y":0.05},{"x":2,"y":0.025},{"x":3,"y":0.0125},{"x":4,"y":0.00625},{"x":5,"y":0.003125},{"x":6,"y":0.0015625}]}],"annotations":[]}}
```

Exponential decay applies $\eta_t = \eta_0 \gamma^t$, where $\gamma$ is a decay factor per epoch $t$. Step decay drops $\eta$ by a factor at fixed intervals.

One common failure mode is decaying $\eta$ too quickly, which traps the model in suboptimal local minima before gradients stabilize.

runs.prompt: what does the sigmoid activation function do?
runs.title: Sigmoid Activation Function
runs.body:
The sigmoid function maps any real-valued number into a smooth range between zero and one.

Its precise mathematical form is given by $\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$, where $z$ is the linear score from the network layer.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"A sigmoid links score to probability","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Linear score","min":-4,"max":4,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Positive probability","min":0,"max":1},"series":[{"label":"Sigmoid","kind":"line","points":[{"x":-4,"y":0.018},{"x":-3,"y":0.047},{"x":-2,"y":0.119},{"x":-1,"y":0.269},{"x":0,"y":0.5},{"x":1,"y":0.731},{"x":2,"y":0.881},{"x":3,"y":0.953},{"x":4,"y":0.982}]}],"annotations":[{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Probability threshold","axis":"y","value":0.5},{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Equivalent score threshold","axis":"x","value":0}]}}
```

Looking at the coordinate plot above, notice how extreme positive scores approach one and extreme negative scores approach zero.

The function saturates at both ends, which causes the vanishing gradient problem during deep network backpropagation.

This squashing behavior makes sigmoid useful for binary classification tasks, as the output can be directly interpreted as a probability. When the input score is exactly zero, the output probability equals $0.5$.

runs.body:
Think about guessing if it will rain today when you look outside at the dark clouds. Your model gives a certain percentage chance for rain, which is like a guess at the truth.

A lower number means your model guessed well and was not surprised by the real world.

When you train an AI, it tries to make this surprise number as small as possible.

It starts at an initial parameter value and calculates the gradient, which points in the direction of the steepest ascent.

By taking a step in the opposite direction of this gradient, the algorithm systematically reduces the loss.

runs.prompt: what is gradient descent?
runs.title: Gradient Descent
runs.body:
Gradient descent is an iterative optimization algorithm used to find the minimum of a function by moving in the direction of steepest descent.

Suppose we want to minimize a loss function $L(w)$ that measures model error given weights $w$. Starting from an initial guess, we compute the gradient, which points toward the greatest rate of increase.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Descent path on quadratic loss","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Weight 1","min":-3,"max":3},"y":{"label":"Weight 2","min":-3,"max":3},"series":[{"label":"Outer loss contour","kind":"line","closed":true,"samples":{"radius":2,"count":16}},{"label":"Inner loss contour","kind":"line","closed":true,"samples":{"radius":1,"count":16}}],"annotations":[{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 1","from":{"x":-1.5,"y":1.1},"to":{"x":-0.9,"y":0.7}},{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 2","from":{"x":-0.9,"y":0.7},"to":{"x":-0.4,"y":0.3}},{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 3","from":{"x":-0.4,"y":0.3},"to":{"x":0,"y":0}}]}}
```

To minimize error, we take steps in the exact opposite direction of the gradient vector. The size of each step is controlled by the learning rate $\alpha$, a hyperparameter that scales the update.

If $\alpha$ is too large, the algorithm overshoots the minimum; if it is too small, convergence takes too many steps.

runs.prompt: what is a learning rate schedule?
runs.title: Learning-rate schedules
runs.body:
Training a neural network requires adjusting model parameters using gradient descent, where the step size is controlled by the learning rate.

Keeping this rate constant can cause training to stall or oscillate around the minimum of the loss function. A learning rate schedule systematically changes this rate over time to improve convergence.

Look at the coordinate plot to see how different decay strategies alter the step size across epochs. Step decay drops the rate by a fixed factor at scheduled intervals, whereas exponential decay reduces it continuously.

By starting with a larger rate, the model quickly navigates rough loss landscapes.

runs.prompt: what is a learning rate schedule?
runs.title: Learning Rate Schedules
runs.body:
Training a neural network requires adjusting parameters via optimization algorithms, where the learning rate $\alpha$ controls step size.

If $\alpha$ remains constant, updates may overshoot minima, so a learning rate schedule reduces $\alpha$ over time to stabilize convergence.

Look for step decay holding rates flat before dropping them abruptly, and exponential decay reducing rates smoothly at every epoch.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Step decay and exponential decay","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Epoch","min":0,"max":6,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Learning rate","min":0.001,"max":0.1,"scale":"log"},"series":[{"label":"Step decay","kind":"step","points":[{"x":0,"y":0.1},{"x":2,"y":0.03},{"x":4,"y":0.01},{"x":6,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"Exponential decay","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0.1},{"x":1,"y":0.05},{"x":2,"y":0.025},{"x":3,"y":0.0125},{"x":4,"y":0.00625},{"x":5,"y":0.003125},{"x":6,"y":0.0015625}]}],"annotations":[]}}
```

Step decay drops the rate by a factor at fixed intervals, whereas exponential decay multiplies the initial rate by an exponential factor $\gamma^{epoch}$.

These adjustments allow large initial steps for fast progress and tiny final steps for precise fine-tuning.

runs.prompt: what is the difference between precision and recall?
runs.title: Precision and Recall
runs.body:
When evaluating a model, we look at how it classifies items into positive and negative outcomes. Consider a medical test for a rare disease where a positive result means the patient has the condition.

Precision measures how many selected items are relevant, while recall measures how many relevant items are selected.

Precision is calculated as $\frac{TP}{TP + FP}$ using true positives and false positives. It answers what proportion of positive identifications was actually correct.

High precision means fewer false alarms when the model predicts a positive outcome.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Confusion Matrix","kind":"matrix","columns":["Pred Positive","Pred Negative"],"rows":[{"heading":"Actual Positive","cells":["True Positive","False Negative"]},{"heading":"Actual Negative","cells":["False Positive","True Negative"]}]}}
```

High recall means the model misses fewer real positive cases in its results.

runs.prompt: what is the difference between precision and recall?
runs.title: Precision and Recall
runs.body:
When evaluating a model, we look at how it classifies items into positive and negative outcomes. Precision asks out of all predicted positives, how many were actually positive.

It is calculated as $\frac{\text{True Positives}}{\text{True Positives} + \text{False Positives}}$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Confusion Matrix","kind":"matrix","columns":["Pred Positive","Pred Negative"],"rows":[{"heading":"Actual Positive","cells":["True Positive","False Negative"]},{"heading":"Actual Negative","cells":["False Positive","True Negative"]}]}}
```

Recall asks out of all actual positives, how many did the model find. It is calculated as $\frac{\text{True Positives}}{\text{True Positives} + \text{False Negatives}}$.

While precision guards against false alarms, recall guards against missed detections.

runs.prompt: what does the sigmoid activation function do?
runs.title: The Sigmoid Activation Function
runs.body:
When a logistic regression model evaluates an email to spot spam, it computes a raw linear score that can range from negative to positive infinity. This unbounded number is hard to interpret directly as a chance of spam.

To make sense of it, the model applies the sigmoid function, which squashes any real-valued number into a neat range between zero and one.

Look at the S-shaped curve on the plot to see how extreme scores flatten out toward probabilities of zero or one. The formula is $\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$, where $z$ is the incoming linear score.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"A sigmoid links score to probability","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Linear score","min":-4,"max":4,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Positive probability","min":0,"max":1},"series":[{"label":"Sigmoid","kind":"line","points":[{"x":-4,"y":0.018},{"x":-3,"y":0.047},{"x":-2,"y":0.119},{"x":-1,"y":0.269},{"x":0,"y":0.5},{"x":1,"y":0.731},{"x":2,"y":0.881},{"x":3,"y":0.953},{"x":4,"y":0.982}]}],"annotations":[{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Probability threshold","axis":"y","value":0.5},{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Equivalent score threshold","axis":"x","value":0}]}}
```

Values far below zero crush down toward zero, while values far above zero saturate near one.

runs.prompt: what does the sigmoid activation function do?
runs.title: The Sigmoid Activation Function
runs.body:
The sigmoid activation function transforms any real-valued number into a probability between $0$ and $1$. Consider a logistic regression model predicting whether an email is spam based on a linear score $z$.

Passing $z$ through the sigmoid function $\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$ squeezes extreme values.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"A sigmoid links score to probability","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Linear score","min":-4,"max":4,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Positive probability","min":0,"max":1},"series":[{"label":"Sigmoid","kind":"line","points":[{"x":-4,"y":0.018},{"x":-3,"y":0.047},{"x":-2,"y":0.119},{"x":-1,"y":0.269},{"x":0,"y":0.5},{"x":1,"y":0.731},{"x":2,"y":0.881},{"x":3,"y":0.953},{"x":4,"y":0.982}]}],"annotations":[{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Probability threshold","axis":"y","value":0.5},{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Equivalent score threshold","axis":"x","value":0}]}}
```

Notice how a score of zero maps exactly to a probability of $0.5$. Positive scores map above $0.5$, while negative scores map below it.

This smooth S-shape lets neural networks handle binary classification by outputting clear likelihoods.

runs.body:
Imagine you have a basket of mixed fruit that you want to sort into clean groups.

Gini impurity is a measure of how often a randomly chosen item from that group would be labeled incorrectly if you randomly labeled it according to the distribution of labels in the group.

A completely pure group where all items belong to a single category has a Gini impurity of zero.

When items are evenly split between different categories, the impurity reaches its highest value because guessing becomes a pure coin toss.

Decision tree algorithms calculate this impurity to decide the best way to split data into cleaner, more organized branches.

runs.prompt: how are attention weights computed?
runs.title: Computing Attention Weights
runs.body:
Attention weights tell a model which words to focus on when looking at a sentence. When reading a word, the model compares it to all other words by taking a dot product of their vectors.

Look at the weights linking the source words to the target word in the diagram below to see how attention distributes across them.


These raw scores are then divided and scaled so they add up to one. This final step turns the raw numbers into probabilities called attention weights.

The heaviest weight sums to one across the connected tokens as shown in the caption.

runs.prompt: how are attention weights computed?
runs.title: How Attention Weights Are Computed
runs.body:
Attention weights tell a model which parts of a text to focus on when processing a word. Think of reading a sentence and glancing back at earlier words to grasp the current meaning.

Look at how the second word connects to the words before it in the diagram below.


The model compares each word to every other word by taking a dot product of their vector representations. These raw scores measure how closely related two words are in context.

Next, the model passes these scores through a softmax function to turn them into positive numbers that sum to one. These final values are the attention weights used to blend the information.

runs.prompt: what is gini impurity
runs.title: Gini Impurity
runs.body:
Gini impurity measures how often a randomly chosen element from a set would be incorrectly labeled if it were randomly labeled according to the distribution of labels in the set.

For a binary classification problem with probability $p$ of the positive class, it is calculated as $I_G(p) = 1 - (p^2 + (1-p)^2)$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Gini Impurity for a Two-Class Node","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Probability $p$ of class 1","min":0,"max":1},"y":{"label":"Gini impurity $I_G(p)$","min":0,"max":0.5},"series":[{"label":"$1 - (p^2 + (1-p)^2)$","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0},{"x":0.1,"y":0.18},{"x":0.2,"y":0.32},{"x":0.3,"y":0.42},{"x":0.4,"y":0.48},{"x":0.5,"y":0.5,"label":"Max impurity $p=0.5$"},{"x":0.6,"y":0.48},{"x":0.7,"y":0.42},{"x":0.8,"y":0.32},{"x":0.9,"y":0.18},{"x":1,"y":0}]}]}}
```

Looking at the plot, impurity is minimized at zero when all elements belong to a single class, representing a pure node.

It reaches its maximum value of $0.5$ when the classes are evenly split with $p = 0.5$, indicating complete uncertainty.

Decision trees use this metric at every split to determine the best feature for separating classes.

runs.prompt: what is gini impurity
runs.title: Gini Impurity in Decision Trees
runs.body:
Gini impurity measures how often a randomly chosen element from a set would be incorrectly labeled if it were randomly labeled according to the distribution of labels in the subset.

Consider a node with 4 positive and 4 negative examples, giving an equal probability $p = 0.5$ for each class. This represents maximum disorder, yielding a high impurity value.

Observe the curve peaking at $0.5$ on the vertical axis when the probability is balanced at $0.5$ on the horizontal axis.

Mathematically, the metric is defined as $I_G(p) = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{J} p_i^2$, where $p_i$ is the probability of a-item $i$ being chosen.

Lower values indicate that the resulting groups are purer and more homogeneous.

runs.title: Skewed distributions and log transforms
runs.body:
When data spans several orders of magnitude, values pile up near zero while a long tail stretches out to the right. This right skewness hides detail among smaller observations.

Applying a logarithmic transformation pulls in that stretched tail by compressing large values. Intervals that span huge gaps on the raw scale become evenly spaced steps after the transformation.

This compression helps reveal patterns across the entire range without altering the underlying rank order of the observations. It is a standard tool for stabilizing variance in modeling.

runs.prompt: What happens to a skewed distribution when we take logs?

Notice how the comparison shows raw values stretched across a wide range versus log values spaced in equal intervals. This compression pulls in extreme outliers and often stabilizes the variance across the range.

While log transforms make patterns more visible, they do not automatically guarantee that the resulting data will be normally distributed.

runs.prompt: How does Bayesian optimization decide which setting to try next?
runs.title: How Bayesian Optimization Picks the Next Trial
runs.body:
Bayesian optimization balances exploring unknown regions and exploiting known good settings by using a probabilistic surrogate model.

It builds a Gaussian process regression model to predict both the expected performance and uncertainty across the parameter space.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Acquisition choice matrix","caption":"Comparing candidates by mean $\\mu$, uncertainty $\\sigma$, and upper confidence bound score.","kind":"matrix","layout":"teaching","columns":["$\\mu,\\sigma$","UCB Score"],"rows":[{"id":"a","heading":"A","cells":["0.70, 0.02","0.72"]},{"id":"b","heading":"B","cells":["0.76, 0.02","0.78"]},{"id":"c","heading":"C","cells":["0.73, 0.10","0.83"]}],"emphasis":{"cells":[{"row":"c","column":1}]}}}
```

An acquisition function translates these predictions into a single score that determines the next trial location. Candidates with high predicted means or high uncertainty receive higher acquisition scores.

Evaluating the upper confidence bound adds an exploration bonus proportional to the predictive standard deviation. Candidate C wins the next trial because its uncertainty bonus outweighs a slightly lower mean.

runs.prompt: How does Bayesian optimization decide which setting to try next?
runs.title: Bayesian Optimization Setting Selection
runs.body:
Bayesian optimization balances exploring unknown regions and exploiting known good settings using an acquisition function.

For example, when tuning tree depths, a surrogate model predicts the mean $\mu$ and uncertainty $\sigma$ for each candidate.


runs.prompt: what is entropy?
runs.title: Entropy in Thermodynamics
runs.body:
Entropy is a fundamental thermodynamic property quantifying the degree of energy dispersal in a system.

The change in entropy $dS$ for a reversible process is defined as $dS = \frac{dQ_{rev}}{T}$, where $dQ_{rev}$ is the heat added reversibly and $T$ is absolute temperature.

Look at the state transformation diagram above to see how adding thermal energy shifts a system from a low entropy state to a dispersed high entropy state.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"State transition of a thermal system","caption":"Transition from an ordered state to a dispersed state via heat addition.","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Initial state","items":["Low entropy","Compact energy"]},"after":{"label":"Final state","items":["High entropy","Dispersed energy"]},"operation":"Add thermal energy $Q$ at temperature $T$"}}
```

This directional limitation prevents perpetual motion machines of the second kind and dictates the arrow of time for macroscopic systems.

It quantifies the number of microscopic configurations consistent with the macroscopic state via $S = k_B \ln \Omega$.

Examine the diagram below to see how adding heat alters the microscopic disorder of the system.

In any spontaneous process, the total entropy of an isolated system always increases or remains constant, expressed as $\Delta S_{\text{total}} \geq 0$.

This directional limitation governs the efficiency limits of thermodynamic cycles and irreversible losses.

runs.title: Population Growth Models
runs.body:
Populations grow through births and immigration, driven by the per capita growth rate $r$. When resources are unlimited, growth follows an exponential curve where population size explodes over time.

Look at the plotted curves to compare unchecked exponential rise against the stabilizing logistic curve.


In reality, limited food and space introduce a carrying capacity $K$ that slows down reproduction as crowding increases.

This gives rise to the logistic growth model, described by the differential equation $\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right)$. As $N$ approaches $K$, growth rate drops near zero, stabilizing the population.

runs.body:
Quantization replaces a smooth range of values with a small set of discrete levels. It is used when storage or transmission can only handle limited bits.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"kind":"coordinate-plot","title":"Illustrative quantization mapping (line approximation)","caption":"Each input integer maps to the nearest even output level","x":{"label":"Input (continuous)","min":0,"max":9},"y":{"label":"Output (quantized)","min":0,"max":8},"series":[{"label":"Quantized output","kind":"line","markers":true,"points":[{"x":0,"y":0},{"x":1,"y":0},{"x":2,"y":2},{"x":3,"y":2},{"x":4,"y":4},{"x":5,"y":4},{"x":6,"y":6},{"x":7,"y":6},{"x":8,"y":8},{"x":9,"y":8}]}]}}
```

A vector database indexes high-dimensional arrays called embeddings to enable fast similarity searching across unstructured data like text and images.

When a query arrives, the system computes metrics like cosine similarity to find the nearest vectors in the spatial index.

runs.prompt: how are attention weights computed?
runs.title: Computing Attention Weights
runs.body:
Attention weights are computed by taking the dot product of a query vector and a set of key vectors, scaling them by the square root of the head dimension $d_k$, and applying a softmax function.

Look for the normalized weights summing to one in the token links diagram below.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Attention weights $w_1+w_2=1$","kind":"token-links","source":["Query","Key"],"target":["Query","Key"],"queries":[{"index":1,"weights":[0.25,0.75]}],"normalized":true}}
```

The exact formula is $\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$. This scaling factor prevents the gradients from vanishing during backpropagation when the dimensions are large.

runs.prompt: how are attention weights computed?
runs.title: Computing Attention Weights
runs.body:
Attention weights scale how much focus a query places on each key in the sequence. Look at the weights linking the tokens to see how scores are distributed.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Attention weights $w_1+w_2=1$","kind":"token-links","source":["Query","Key"],"target":["Query","Key"],"queries":[{"index":1,"weights":[0.2,0.8]}],"normalized":true}}
```

Formally, given queries $Q$, keys $K$, and values $V$ with dimension $d_k$, the mechanism computes the dot product of queries and keys.

This raw score is scaled by $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}$ to prevent vanishing gradients in high dimensions.

A softmax function then normalizes these scaled scores into probabilities that sum to one. These final weights multiply the value matrix $V$ to produce the attended output vector.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy loss?
runs.title: Cross Entropy Loss
runs.body:
Cross entropy loss measures the dissimilarity between two probability distributions, typically the true labels and the predicted probabilities from a classification model.

For a single binary classification instance, the formula is defined as $L = -y \log(p) - (1-y) \log(1-p)$, where $y$ is the true label and $p$ is the predicted probability.

Notice how the penalty approaches infinity as the prediction becomes confidently wrong. Look at the curves in the plot to see how loss increases sharply when $p$ approaches zero for a true positive.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Cross-entropy depends on the true label","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Predicted positive probability","min":0.01,"max":0.99,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Loss","min":0,"max":5},"series":[{"label":"True class 1","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":4.605},{"x":0.1,"y":2.303},{"x":0.25,"y":1.386},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":0.288},{"x":0.9,"y":0.105},{"x":0.99,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"True class 0","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":0.01},{"x":0.1,"y":0.105},{"x":0.25,"y":0.288},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":1.386},{"x":0.9,"y":2.303},{"x":0.99,"y":4.605}]}],"annotations":[]}}
```

In practice, clipping predicted probabilities near zero and one is essential to prevent numerical overflow from $\log(0)$.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy loss?
runs.title: Cross Entropy Loss
runs.body:
Cross entropy loss measures the performance of a classification model whose output is a probability value between $0$ and $1$.

For a single binary decision, the formula is $L = -y \log(p) - (1-y) \log(1-p)$, where $y$ is the true label and $p$ is the predicted probability.

Notice how the penalty grows steeply as the prediction gets more confidently wrong.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Cross-entropy depends on the true label","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Predicted positive probability","min":0.01,"max":0.99,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Loss","min":0,"max":5},"series":[{"label":"True class 1","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":4.605},{"x":0.1,"y":2.303},{"x":0.25,"y":1.386},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":0.288},{"x":0.9,"y":0.105},{"x":0.99,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"True class 0","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":0.01},{"x":0.1,"y":0.105},{"x":0.25,"y":0.288},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":1.386},{"x":0.9,"y":2.303},{"x":0.99,"y":4.605}]}],"annotations":[]}}
```

When the true label $y$ is $1$, the second term vanishes and the loss simplifies to $-\log(p)$. If the model predicts $p = 0.01$, the loss surges past $4.0$, heavily penalizing confident mistakes.

Conversely, when $y$ is $0$, the first term vanishes and the loss becomes $-\log(1-p)$.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy loss?
runs.title: Cross Entropy Loss
runs.body:
When a computer program tries to guess which category an item belongs to, it gives a list of percentages for each possible choice.

Cross entropy loss is a score that measures how wrong these percentage guesses are compared to the true answer.

Think of it like a penalty score where a confident, correct guess gets a tiny penalty, but a confident, wrong guess gets a massive penalty.

```rh-diagram

```

To figure out this penalty, the formula looks at the exact probability the model assigned to the right answer. If the model is certain and correct, the penalty drops close to zero.

If the model gets it completely wrong, the penalty shoots up toward infinity.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy loss?
runs.title: Cross-Entropy Loss
runs.body:
When a model predicts a cat picture has a probability $p = 0.9$ of being a cat, but the true label is $y = 1$, we measure the surprise using cross entropy loss.

The formula for a single binary observation is $L = -y \log(p) - (1-y) \log(1-p)$, penalizing confident wrong guesses heavily.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Cross-entropy depends on the true label","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Predicted positive probability","min":0.01,"max":0.99,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Loss","min":0,"max":5},"series":[{"label":"True class 1","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":4.605},{"x":0.1,"y":2.303},{"x":0.25,"y":1.386},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":0.288},{"x":0.9,"y":0.105},{"x":0.99,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"True class 0","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":0.01},{"x":0.1,"y":0.105},{"x":0.25,"y":0.288},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":1.386},{"x":0.9,"y":2.303},{"x":0.99,"y":4.605}]}],"annotations":[]}}
```

Looking at the coordinate plot above, when the true class is $1$, predicting near zero sends the loss toward infinity as $-\log(p)$ grows.

Conversely, predicting near one drops the loss close to zero because $-\log(1) = 0$. This mechanism drives neural network training by creating steep gradients for mistakes.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy loss?
runs.title: Cross-Entropy Loss
runs.body:
Cross-entropy loss measures how wrong a classification model is by penalizing confident wrong predictions heavily.

For example, if an image is actually a dog with true label $y = 1$, and our model predicts a positive probability $p = 0.9$, the penalty is very small.

The mechanism relies on the negative log of the predicted probability for the correct class, written as $L = -y \log p - (1-y) \log(1-p)$.

This logarithmic curve ensures that predicting $0$ when the truth is $1$ results in infinite loss.

runs.prompt: what is batch normalization?
runs.title: Batch Normalization
runs.body:
Batch normalization stabilizes deep neural networks by normalizing layer inputs for every training batch. This reduces internal covariate shift, allowing higher learning rates and faster convergence.

Look at the transformation above to see how raw activations are centered, scaled, and adjusted with learnable parameters $\gamma$ and $\beta$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Batch normalization steps","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Input values","items":["Raw activations $x_i$"]},"after":{"label":"Normalized values","items":["Scaled outputs $y_i$"]},"operation":"Subtract mean $\\mu_B$, divide by $\\sqrt{\\sigma_B^2 + \\epsilon}$, then scale and shift."}}
```

For a mini-batch $B$, the network first computes the mean $\mu_B$ and variance $\sigma_B^2$ of the current activations. It then normalizes the data and applies scale and shift parameters to retain expressive power.

runs.prompt: what is batch normalization?
runs.title: Batch Normalization
runs.body:
Training deep neural networks is difficult because the distribution of each layer's inputs changes during training, a phenomenon called internal covariate shift.

To stabilize learning, batch normalization standardizes layer inputs across each mini-batch.

Look at the normalization operation shown in the diagram to see how raw inputs are centered and scaled using batch statistics.

For a mini-batch $B$, the layer computes the empirical mean $\mu_B$ and variance $\sigma_B^2$, then normalizes the activations using a small constant $\epsilon$ for numerical stability.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Normalize layer inputs","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Original activations","items":["Mean $\\mu_B$","Variance $\\sigma_B^2$"]},"after":{"label":"Normalized outputs","items":["Zero mean","Unit variance $\\gamma, \\beta$"]},"operation":"$\\hat{x}_i = \\frac{x_i - \\mu_B}{\\sqrt{\\sigma_B^2 + \\epsilon}}$"}}
```

Finally, two learnable parameters $\gamma$ and $\beta$ scale and shift the normalized values so the network can retain its expressive power.

runs.prompt: how does dropout work?

runs.body:
During neural network training, dropout randomly deactivates hidden units to prevent overfitting. Look at the transformation steps to see how training and inference differ.

Each training step drops units with probability $1-p$, forcing the network to learn redundant representations. At inference time, all units remain active while weights are scaled by the keep rate $p$.

This ensures the expected output magnitude matches training.

runs.prompt: how does cross-validation detect overfitting?

runs.prompt: how does cross-validation detect overfitting?
runs.title: Cross-Validation and Overfitting
runs.body:
Cross-validation detects overfitting by partitioning the dataset into $k$ subsets, training on $k-1$ folds, and testing on the held-out fold.

This rotation ensures every data point acts as an unseen test sample at least once.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Model Error Across Folds","caption":"Validation error exceeds training error when overfitting occurs.","kind":"bar-chart","unit":"MSE","bars":[{"label":"Training Error","value":0.12},{"label":"Validation Error","value":0.45}]}}
```

When training error is low but validation error spikes, the discrepancy exposes memorization of noise rather than true generalization.

The generalization error estimate $\hat{E}$ is averaged across all folds to yield a reliable performance metric.

Pruning model complexity or adding regularization resolves the gap when validation scores diverge from training benchmarks.

runs.prompt: How do attention scores turn into weights?
runs.title: Converting Attention Scores to Weights
runs.body:
Attention scores $s_j = q \cdot k_j$ are raw dot products that can take any real value and lack an upper bound.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Softmax over scores","caption":"Compute $a_j=\\exp(s_j)/\\sum_i\\exp(s_i)$ to ensure weights sum to one.","kind":"token-links","source":["key1","key2"],"target":["key1","key2"],"queries":[{"index":0,"weights":[0.731,0.269]}],"normalized":true}}
```

To turn these unconstrained scores into a probability distribution, the softmax function exponentiates each score and divides by the sum of all exponentiated scores.

This operation guarantees that every resulting weight $a_j$ is strictly positive and that all weights sum to exactly one across the sequence.

runs.prompt: How do attention scores turn into weights?
runs.title: Converting Attention Scores to Weights
runs.body:
Raw attention scores $s_j$ are converted into probability weights using the softmax function. This operation exponentiates each score to ensure positivity and divides by the sum across all keys.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Attention weights $w_1+w_2=1$","caption":"Compute $a_j=\\exp(s_j)/\\sum_i\\exp(s_i)$ over keys. The displayed weights sum to one.","kind":"token-links","source":["key1","key2"],"target":["key1","key2"],"queries":[{"index":0,"weights":[0.25,0.75]}],"normalized":true}}
```

The resulting weights $a_j = \frac{\exp(s_j)}{\sum_i \exp(s_i)}$ always sum to one. This creates a convex combination of values used in downstream representations.

A central failure mode is attending to irrelevant padding tokens when masks are omitted. In practice, scaling by $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}$ prevents vanishing gradients during training.

runs.prompt: Why does a transformer use more than one attention head?
runs.title: Multi-Head Attention in Transformers
runs.body:
Transformers use multi-head attention to project queries, keys, and values into different representation subspaces simultaneously.

Given $H$ heads, the input vector of dimension $d_{\text{model}}$ is split into projections of dimension $d_k = d_{\text{model}} / H$. Each head independently computes scaled dot-product attention in its own subspace.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Attention weights by head and token","caption":"Both heads query sat. Head A puts the most weight on cat, and Head B puts the most on the first the.","kind":"bar-chart","variant":"grouped","categories":["1. the","2. cat","3. sat","4. on","5. the","6. mat"],"series":[{"label":"Head A","values":[0.052,0.65,0.192,0.059,0.02,0.027]},{"label":"Head B","values":[0.388,0.175,0.093,0.049,0.077,0.218]}]}}
```

This parallel setup allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions.

As shown above, distinct heads specialize in different linguistic relations for the same query token.

Failing to use multiple heads restricts the model to a single averaging operation over context.

runs.prompt: How does a transformer get a match score between words?
runs.title: Scaled dot-product attention scores
runs.body:
Transformers compute match scores between words using the dot product of query vectors and key vectors. For a query $q$ and keys $k_j$, the raw alignment is $q \cdot k_j$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Scaled dot-product scores for sat","caption":"Use $s_j=(q\\cdot k_j)/\\sqrt{d_k}$ for each key, with $d_k=2$ shown out of 256 entries.","kind":"matrix","layout":"teaching","columns":["Dot product","Scaled score"],"rows":[{"id":"k1","heading":"the 1","cells":["-0.539","-0.381"]},{"id":"k2","heading":"cat 2","cells":["3.034","2.145"]},{"id":"k3","heading":"sat 3","cells":["1.306","0.923"]},{"id":"k4","heading":"on 4","cells":["-0.361","-0.255"]},{"id":"k5","heading":"the 5","cells":["-1.924","-1.36"]},{"id":"k6","heading":"mat 6","cells":["-1.486","-1.051"]}]}}
```

To prevent gradients from vanishing when dimensionality $d_k$ is large, this product is scaled by the square root of the key dimension $\sqrt{d_k}$. The resulting score formula is $s_j = \frac{q \cdot k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}$.

runs.prompt: How does a transformer get a match score between words?
runs.title: Transformer Word Match Scores
runs.body:
Transformers compute match scores between words using the dot product of query and key vectors. For any query vector $q$ and key vector $k_j$, the raw alignment score is given by their inner product $q \cdot k_j$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Scaled dot-product scores for sat","caption":"Use $s_j=(q\\cdot k_j)/\\sqrt{d_k}$ for each key, with $d_k=2$ shown out of 256 entries.","kind":"matrix","layout":"teaching","columns":["Dot product","Scaled score"],"rows":[{"id":"k1","heading":"the 1","cells":["-0.539","-0.381"]},{"id":"k2","heading":"cat 2","cells":["3.034","2.145"]},{"id":"k3","heading":"sat 3","cells":["1.306","0.923"]}]}}
```

To prevent gradients from vanishing when dimensionality $d_k$ is large, this dot product is scaled down by the square root of the key dimension.

The final scaled score equation is expressed as $s_j = \frac{q \cdot k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}$.

This division stabilizes the softmax function applied immediately afterward, ensuring stable training dynamics across deep self-attention layers.

runs.prompt: what is maximum likelihood estimation?
runs.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation
runs.body:
Maximum likelihood estimation finds parameter values that maximize the likelihood function for observed data.

Given independent and identically distributed data $x_1, \dots, x_n$, the joint probability density function defines the likelihood as $L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i | \theta)$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Likelihood function $L(\\theta)$","caption":"The maximum likelihood estimate $\\hat{\\theta}$ maximizes the probability of observing the data.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Parameter $\\theta$","min":0,"max":10},"y":{"label":"Likelihood $L(\\theta)$","min":0,"max":1},"series":[{"label":"$L(\\theta)$","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0.1},{"x":2,"y":0.4},{"x":4,"y":0.8},{"x":5,"y":0.95,"label":"Maximum $\\hat{\\theta}$"},{"x":6,"y":0.85},{"x":8,"y":0.4},{"x":10,"y":0.1}]}]}}
```

In practice, we maximize the log-likelihood function $\log L(\theta)$ instead of the raw product to simplify calculations.

Differentiating with respect to $\theta$ yields the score function, and setting it to zero gives the maximum likelihood estimator $\hat{\theta}$.

A primary failure mode is overfitting when models grow too complex for the sample size.

runs.prompt: what is maximum likelihood estimation?
runs.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation
runs.body:
Maximum likelihood estimation finds parameter values that maximize the likelihood function for observed data.

Given a sample of independent and identically distributed observations $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ from a probability density function $f(x | \theta)$, the joint likelihood is $L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i | \theta)$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Likelihood function $L(\\theta)$","caption":"The maximum likelihood estimator $\\hat{\\theta}$ maximizes the likelihood of observing the given data.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Parameter $\\theta$","min":0,"max":10},"y":{"label":"Likelihood $L(\\theta)$","min":0,"max":1},"series":[{"label":"$L(\\theta)$","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0.05},{"x":2,"y":0.2},{"x":4,"y":0.6},{"x":5,"y":0.9,"label":"$\\hat{\\theta}$"},{"x":6,"y":0.6},{"x":8,"y":0.2},{"x":10,"y":0.05}]}]}}
```

In practice, it is easier to maximize the natural logarithm of the likelihood function, known as the log-likelihood function $\ln L(\theta)$.

Setting the derivative of the log-likelihood with respect to the parameter $\theta$ to zero yields the score equation $\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \ln L(\theta) = 0$.

runs.prompt: what is overfitting?
runs.title: Understanding Overfitting
runs.body:
Overfitting happens when a model learns the training data too well, capturing noise instead of the underlying pattern. This causes poor generalization to unseen data.

Look at the coordinate plot to see how the complex model weaves through every training point while missing the held-out point entirely.

To prevent this issue, practitioners use regularization techniques like $L_1$ and $L_2$ penalties or early stopping during training. These methods restrict model complexity, ensuring robust performance on new data.

runs.prompt: why does a bootstrap sample contain only about 63% of the unique training rows?

runs.body:
When building a random forest, each tree trains on a bootstrap sample created by drawing $n$ rows with replacement from a dataset of size $n$.

Look at the curve in the plot to see how the chance a specific row is left out approaches $1/e$ as $n$ grows large. Every time we draw a row, the probability it is not our chosen row is $1 - \frac{1}{n}$.

Because draws are independent, the chance that our row is missed across all $n$ draws is $(1 - \frac{1}{n})^n$.


As $n$ approaches infinity, this expression converges to the mathematical constant $1/e$, which is approximately $0.368$ or $36.8$ percent. The complement of this omission probability gives the expected unique coverage.

runs.prompt: how does Gini impurity change as the fraction of one class goes from 0 to 1, compared with entropy?
runs.title: Gini impurity vs entropy
runs.body:
When building decision trees, nodes split data to maximize purity. We measure node disorder using Gini impurity and entropy.

Notice how both curves start at zero when $p = 0$ or $p = 1$, rising to a peak at $p = 0.5$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Gini impurity and entropy","caption":"Worked example. Gini impurity is $2p(1-p)$ and entropy is $-p\\log_2 p-(1-p)\\log_2(1-p)$. Samples rounded to 3 decimals.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Class fraction p","min":0,"max":1},"y":{"label":"Impurity score","min":0,"max":1},"series":[{"label":"Gini impurity","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0},{"x":0.2,"y":0.32},{"x":0.4,"y":0.48},{"x":0.5,"y":0.5,"label":"Gini peak"},{"x":0.6,"y":0.48},{"x":0.8,"y":0.32},{"x":1,"y":0}]},{"label":"Entropy (bits)","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0},{"x":0.2,"y":0.722},{"x":0.4,"y":0.971},{"x":0.5,"y":1,"label":"Entropy peak"},{"x":0.6,"y":0.971},{"x":0.8,"y":0.722},{"x":1,"y":0}]}]}}
```

Gini impurity calculates the probability of misclassifying a randomly chosen element, defined as $G(p) = 2p(1-p)$. Entropy measures average information content using $H(p) = -p\log_2 p - (1-p)\log_2(1-p)$.

Both metrics reach their maximum when classes are evenly split, but entropy scales up to $1$ bit while Gini peaks at $0.5$.

runs.prompt: how do I compute the Gini impurity on both sides of a split and the information gain?
runs.title: Computing Gini Impurity and Information Gain
runs.body:
To measure node purity, we compute the Gini impurity for each side of a split using the formula $1 - \sum p_i^2$, where $p_i$ is the probability of class $i$.

For example, if a node has four items of class zero and zero items of class one, its Gini impurity is zero.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Gini after the root split","caption":"Worked example combining child Ginis in proportion to their sizes.","kind":"matrix","columns":["Class 0","Class 1","Gini","Weight"],"rows":[{"heading":"Left","cells":["4","0","0","0.5"]},{"heading":"Right","cells":["1","3","0.375","0.5"]},{"heading":"After","cells":["—","—","0.1875","1"]}]}}
```

When a node splits into left and children, we combine their impurities using a weighted average based on node sizes.

Information gain is then calculated as the parent impurity minus this weighted child impurity sum, showing how much uncertainty the split removes.

runs.prompt: How does a transformer turn scores into a guess for the next word?
runs.title: Transformer Next-Word Softmax
runs.body:
When predicting the next word, a transformer computes raw numerical values called logits for every candidate in its vocabulary.

These scores measure how well each candidate fits the current context after processing prior tokens.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Vocabulary logits after the cat sat","caption":"A linear layer gives each word in the toy vocabulary a raw score.","kind":"bar-chart","unit":"score","bars":[{"label":"the","value":0.501},{"label":"cat","value":-0.108},{"label":"sat","value":0.78},{"label":"on","value":1.745},{"label":"mat","value":0.201},{"label":"slept","value":-0.495}]}}
```

To turn these raw scores into valid probabilities, the model applies the softmax function across all vocabulary logits.

Softmax exponentiates each score and divides it by the sum of all exponentiated scores, ensuring the results sum to one.

Looking at the bar heights, the word on receives the highest score and therefore the highest probability.

The model then samples from this probability distribution or picks the highest-scoring candidate as its final guess.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy
runs.title: Cross-Entropy Loss Function
runs.body:
Cross-entropy loss measures the difference between two probability distributions, typically the true labels $y$ and the predicted probabilities $\hat{y}$.

For a single binary classification instance, the formula is $H(y,\hat{y}) = -y \log(\hat{y}) - (1-y) \log(1-\hat{y})$.

Observe the penalty curves in the coordinate plot below as predictions diverge from reality.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Cross-entropy depends on the true label","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Predicted positive probability","min":0.01,"max":0.99,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Loss","min":0,"max":5},"series":[{"label":"True class 1","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":4.605},{"x":0.1,"y":2.303},{"x":0.25,"y":1.386},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":0.288},{"x":0.9,"y":0.105},{"x":0.99,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"True class 0","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":0.01},{"x":0.1,"y":0.105},{"x":0.25,"y":0.288},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":1.386},{"x":0.9,"y":2.303},{"x":0.99,"y":4.605}]}],"annotations":[]}}
```

When the true label is $1$, the loss approaches infinity as the prediction $\hat{y}$ approaches $0$, penalizing confident wrong answers heavily.

This logarithmic scaling ensures that models experience steep gradients when they are wrong with high confidence.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy
runs.title: Cross-Entropy Loss Function
runs.body:
Cross-entropy measures the difference between two probability distributions, typically the true labels and the model predictions.

For a single binary event, the formula is $H(p, q) = -(y \log(p) + (1-y) \log(1-p))$, where $y$ is the true binary label and $p$ is the predicted probability.

Observe how the penalty surges as the prediction becomes confidently wrong in the coordinate plot below.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Cross-entropy loss curves for binary classification","caption":"Loss grows as the predicted probability diverges from the true label.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Predicted positive probability $p$","min":0.01,"max":0.99,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Loss","min":0,"max":5},"series":[{"label":"True class 1","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":4.605},{"x":0.25,"y":1.386},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":0.288},{"x":0.99,"y":0.01}]}]}}
```

When $y = 1$, the loss simplifies to $-\log(p)$, penalizing probabilities approaching zero with infinite cost. Conversely, when $y = 0$, the loss becomes $-\log(1-p)$, heavily penalizing false positives.

runs.prompt: what is gradient descent?
runs.title: Gradient Descent Optimization
runs.body:
Gradient descent is an iterative optimization algorithm used to find the minimum of a function by following the negative of its gradient.

The parameter update rule is defined as $\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \nabla L(\theta_t)$, where $\theta$ represents the weights, $\eta$ is the learning rate, and $L(\theta)$ is the loss function.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"A descent path on a quadratic loss","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the steps taken to minimise loss.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Weight 1","min":-3,"max":3,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Weight 2","min":-3,"max":3},"series":[{"label":"Outer loss contour","kind":"line","closed":true,"samples":{"radius":2,"count":16}},{"label":"Inner loss contour","kind":"line","closed":true,"samples":{"radius":1,"count":16}}],"annotations":[{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 1","from":{"x":-1.5,"y":1.1},"to":{"x":-0.9,"y":0.7}},{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 2","from":{"x":-0.9,"y":0.7},"to":{"x":-0.4,"y":0.3}},{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 3","from":{"x":-0.4,"y":0.3},"to":{"x":0,"y":0}}]}}
```

Notice in the plot how successive vector steps cross loss contours perpendicularly to converge toward the minimum at the origin.

A primary failure mode in practice is setting the learning rate too high, which causes the updates to overshoot the minimum and diverge entirely.

runs.prompt: what is gradient descent?
runs.title: Gradient Descent Optimization
runs.body:
Gradient descent minimizes a loss function $\mathcal{L}(w)$ by iteratively moving parameters in the direction of steepest descent.

The parameter update rule is given by $w_{t+1} = w_t - \eta \nabla \mathcal{L}(w_t)$, where $\eta$ represents the learning rate.

Observe the vectors in descending across the loss contours toward the central minimum at the origin.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"A descent path on a quadratic loss","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the steps converging to the minimum.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Weight 1","min":-3,"max":3},"y":{"label":"Weight 2","min":-3,"max":3},"series":[{"label":"Outer loss contour","kind":"line","closed":true,"samples":{"radius":2,"count":16}},{"label":"Inner loss contour","kind":"line","closed":true,"samples":{"radius":1,"count":16}}],"annotations":[{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 1","from":{"x":-1.5,"y":1.1},"to":{"x":-0.9,"y":0.7}},{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 2","from":{"x":-0.9,"y":0.7},"to":{"x":-0.4,"y":0.3}},{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 3","from":{"x":-0.4,"y":0.3},"to":{"x":0,"y":0}}]}}
```

Choosing an appropriate learning rate is critical for convergence. If $\eta$ is too large, the updates will overshoot and diverge; if it is too small, training becomes excessively slow.

runs.prompt: what is a learning rate schedule?
runs.title: Learning Rate Schedules
runs.body:
A learning rate schedule alters the step size during training to balance fast initial progress with precise convergence near the minimum.

Instead of keeping the rate constant, it reduces $\eta_t$ as epochs advance according to a predetermined mathematical function.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Learning-rate schedules share an epoch axis","caption":"Illustrative values; step decay drops flat while exponential decay curves smoothly.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Epoch","min":0,"max":6,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Learning rate","min":0.001,"max":0.1,"scale":"log"},"series":[{"label":"Step decay","kind":"step","points":[{"x":0,"y":0.1},{"x":2,"y":0.03},{"x":4,"y":0.01},{"x":6,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"Exponential decay","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0.1},{"x":1,"y":0.05},{"x":2,"y":0.025},{"x":3,"y":0.0125},{"x":4,"y":0.00625},{"x":5,"y":0.003125},{"x":6,"y":0.0015625}]}],"annotations":[]}}
```

Step decay multiplies the base rate by a factor like $0.1$ at fixed epoch milestones, creating plateaus followed by sudden drops.

Exponential decay continuously scales the rate at epoch $t$ via $\eta_t = \eta_0 \gamma^t$, where $\gamma < 1$ controls the decay speed.

Choosing the right schedule prevents training stagnation and oscillation around the loss minimum.

runs.prompt: what is a learning rate schedule?
runs.title: Learning Rate Schedules
runs.body:
A learning rate schedule dynamically adjusts the step size $\alpha_t$ during training to balance fast initial progress with fine convergence.

By lowering the rate over time, gradient descent avoids overshooting optimal minima as losses plateau.

Notice how the step decay and exponential decay curves trace different paths across epochs.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Learning-rate schedules share an epoch axis","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Epoch","min":0,"max":6,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Learning rate","min":0.001,"max":0.1,"scale":"log"},"series":[{"label":"Step decay","kind":"step","points":[{"x":0,"y":0.1},{"x":2,"y":0.03},{"x":4,"y":0.01},{"x":6,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"Exponential decay","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0.1},{"x":1,"y":0.05},{"x":2,"y":0.025},{"x":3,"y":0.0125},{"x":4,"y":0.00625},{"x":5,"y":0.003125},{"x":6,"y":0.0015625}]}],"annotations":[]}}
```

Common formulations include exponential decay $\alpha_t = \alpha_0 \gamma^t$ and step decay, which drops the rate by a factor at fixed intervals.

In practice, improper schedules lead to oscillating validation loss or premature stagnation.

runs.prompt: what is the difference between precision and recall?
runs.title: Precision versus Recall
runs.body:
Precision asks how many selected items are relevant, while recall asks how many relevant items are selected. In classification tasks, these metrics trade off depending on the decision threshold of the model.

Look at the matrix below to see how true positives relate to false positives and false negatives.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Confusion Matrix","caption":"Precision is $TP / (TP + FP)$ and Recall is $TP / (TP + FN)$.","kind":"matrix","columns":["Predicted Positive","Predicted Negative"],"rows":[{"heading":"Actual Positive","cells":["True Positive (TP)","False Negative (FN)"]},{"heading":"Actual Negative","cells":["False Positive (FP)","True Negative (TN)"]}]}}
```

Precision is defined as $\frac{TP}{TP + FP}$ and measures exactness by penalizing false alarms. High precision means that when the model predicts positive, it is almost always correct.

Recall is defined as $\frac{TP}{TP + FN}$ and measures completeness by penalizing missed positive cases. High recall means the model successfully captures nearly all actual positive instances in the data.

runs.prompt: what does the sigmoid activation function do?
runs.title: The Sigmoid Activation Function
runs.body:
The sigmoid activation function maps any real-valued number into a bounded range between zero and one. Its mathematical formula is given by $\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"A sigmoid links score to probability","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Linear score","min":-4,"max":4,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Positive probability","min":0,"max":1},"series":[{"label":"Sigmoid","kind":"line","points":[{"x":-4,"y":0.018},{"x":-3,"y":0.047},{"x":-2,"y":0.119},{"x":-1,"y":0.269},{"x":0,"y":0.5},{"x":1,"y":0.731},{"x":2,"y":0.881},{"x":3,"y":0.953},{"x":4,"y":0.982}]}],"annotations":[{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Probability threshold","axis":"y","value":0.5},{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Equivalent score threshold","axis":"x","value":0}]}}
```

This squashing property makes it useful for turning unconstrained linear scores into probabilities.

When the input is large and positive, the output approaches one; when it is large and negative, the output approaches zero.

A major limit of the sigmoid function in deep networks is vanishing gradients. For very high or very low inputs, the derivative $\sigma'(x) = \sigma(x)(1 - \sigma(x))$ drops close to zero, halting backpropagation.

The sigmoid function squashes any real-valued number into a bounded range between zero and one. Its mathematical formula is defined precisely as $\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$.
