runs.prompt: what is cross entropy
runs.title: What is cross entropy?
runs.body:
Imagine you are checking weather forecasts to see if it will rain today. Cross entropy is a way to measure how surprised you are by a forecast when you finally see what happens.

Look at the comparison table to see how a real event is matched against a machine guess.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Comparing real labels and machine guesses","kind":"comparison","columns":[{"heading":"Actual event","items":["The email is spam","Probability is 1.0"]},{"heading":"Model guess","items":["Machine thinks 0.8 sure","Probability is 0.8"]}]}}
```

If the forecast says there is zero chance of rain and it pours, you feel very surprised. Cross entropy puts a large number on that surprise to show the model made a poor guess.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy
runs.title: Cross-Entropy Loss
runs.body:
Suppose a model predicts a probability $p$ for an event. Cross-entropy measures the surprise or inefficiency of using that prediction when the true label is $y$.

The loss formula for a single binary decision is $H = -y \log p - (1-y) \log (1-p)$. This penalizes confident wrong guesses heavily.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Cross-entropy depends on the true label","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Predicted positive probability","min":0.01,"max":0.99,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Loss","min":0,"max":5},"series":[{"label":"True class 1","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":4.605},{"x":0.1,"y":2.303},{"x":0.25,"y":1.386},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":0.288},{"x":0.9,"y":0.105},{"x":0.99,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"True class 0","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":0.01},{"x":0.1,"y":0.105},{"x":0.25,"y":0.288},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":1.386},{"x":0.9,"y":2.303},{"x":0.99,"y":4.605}]}],"annotations":[]}}
```

When the true label $y=1$, predicting a low probability $p$ causes the loss to approach infinity. Conversely, a confident correct prediction yields a loss near zero.

This metric drives gradient descent in logistic regression and neural network classifiers. By minimizing this loss, models align their predicted probabilities with reality.

runs.prompt: what is the difference between precision and recall?
runs.title: Precision and Recall
runs.body:
In binary classification, models predict positive or negative outcomes. To measure success beyond simple accuracy, we use precision and recall. These two metrics evaluate different types of errors a model makes.

Precision measures how many of the positively predicted items were actually correct. It focuses on minimizing false positives, making it crucial when false alarms are costly.

The formula is $\frac{\text{True Positives}}{\text{True Positives} + \text{False Positives}}$.

Recall measures how many of the actual positive items the model managed to catch. It focuses on minimizing false negatives, ensuring we do not miss real events.

runs.prompt: what is gini impurity
runs.title: Gini Impurity in Decision Trees
runs.body:
Gini impurity measures how often a randomly chosen element from a set would be incorrectly labeled if it were randomly labeled according to the distribution of labels in the subset.

Consider a leaf node containing four blue items and one red item, where the probability of picking a blue item is $p = 0.8$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Gini Impurity for a Binary Node","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Probability of positive class (p)","min":0,"max":1},"y":{"label":"Gini Impurity","min":0,"max":0.5},"series":[{"label":"$1 - p^2 - (1-p)^2$","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0},{"x":0.2,"y":0.32},{"x":0.4,"y":0.48},{"x":0.5,"y":0.5,"label":"Max impurity at p=0.5"},{"x":0.6,"y":0.48},{"x":0.8,"y":0.32},{"x":1,"y":0}]}]}}
```

The curve shows the quadratic penalty peaking at $0.5$ when classes are evenly split and dropping to zero when pure.

The formal formula for a node with $J$ classes is calculated as $I_G(p) = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{J} p_i^2$, summing the squared probabilities of each class.

Decision tree algorithms evaluate potential splits by computing the weighted sum of child impurities.

runs.prompt: How does Bayesian optimization decide which setting to try next?

runs.body:
Bayesian optimization finds the best setting of a black-box function by balancing exploitation of known good areas with exploration of uncertain ones.

It builds a surrogate model, typically a Gaussian process, mapping inputs to a predicted mean $\mu$ and uncertainty $\sigma$.

An acquisition function uses these predictions to score every candidate setting. A common choice is upper confidence bound, calculating $\mu + k\sigma$ to reward both high predicted performance and high uncertainty.

runs.prompt: what is entropy?
runs.title: Understanding Entropy in Thermodynamics
runs.body:
Entropy is a fundamental thermodynamic property measuring the number of microscopic configurations corresponding to a macroscopic state.

The precise definition is given by Boltzmann's formula $S = k_B \ln \Omega$, where $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant and $\Omega$ is the multiplicity of microstates.

Look at this transformation to see how thermal input increases disorder.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Entropy change in a phase transition","caption":"During melting, heat $Q$ enters at temperature $T$, increasing system entropy by $\\Delta S = \\frac{Q}{T}$.","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Ordered state","items":["Ice crystal lattice"]},"after":{"label":"Disordered state","items":["Liquid water"]},"operation":"Add thermal energy"}}
```

In any isolated system, the second law of thermodynamics requires that total entropy never decreases, expressed as $\Delta S \ge 0$.

This continuous growth establishes a preferred direction for spontaneous physical processes, known colloquially as the arrow of time.

runs.prompt: what is quantization?

Post-training quantization applies this transformation directly to a pre-trained model without retraining.

runs.prompt: how are attention weights computed?
runs.title: Computing Attention Weights
runs.body:
Attention weights derive from the scaled dot-product of query and key vectors. Look at the weight distribution in the diagram below to see how a query attends to keys.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Attention weights $w_1+w_2=1$","kind":"token-links","source":["Query","Key"],"target":["Query","Key"],"queries":[{"index":1,"weights":[0.25,0.75]}],"normalized":true}}
```

Given queries $Q$, keys $K$, and values $V$, the operation computes $\text{softmax}(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}})V$. The scaling factor $\sqrt{d_k}$ prevents gradients from vanishing as the dimension grows large.

runs.prompt: how are attention weights computed?
runs.title: Computing Attention Weights
runs.body:
Attention weights are derived from the scaled dot-product of queries and keys. Given query vector $q$ and key vector $k$ of dimension $d_k$, the weight is computed as $\text{softmax}(\frac{q k^T}{\sqrt{d_k}})$.

Observe how the dot products are scaled by $\sqrt{d_k}$ and normalized across tokens in the token links diagram below.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Attention weights $w_1+w_2=1$","kind":"token-links","source":["Query","Key"],"target":["Query","Key"],"queries":[{"index":1,"weights":[0.25,0.75]}],"normalized":true}}
```

Dividing by the square root of the dimension prevents vanishing gradients when $d_k$ is large. The softmax function then maps these raw scores into a probability distribution summing to one.

This distribution dictates how much focus the model places on different parts of the input sequence during representation updates.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy loss?
runs.title: Cross Entropy Loss
runs.body:
Cross entropy loss measures the dissimilarity between two probability distributions, typically the true labels and the model predictions.

For binary classification, it is defined as $L = -y \log(p) - (1-y) \log(1-p)$, where $y$ is the true label and $p$ is the predicted probability.

Observe how the penalty curves steeply upward as the prediction diverges from the true label in the plot below.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Cross-entropy depends on the true label","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Predicted positive probability","min":0.01,"max":0.99,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Loss","min":0,"max":5},"series":[{"label":"True class 1","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":4.605},{"x":0.1,"y":2.303},{"x":0.25,"y":1.386},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":0.288},{"x":0.9,"y":0.105},{"x":0.99,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"True class 0","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":0.01},{"x":0.1,"y":0.105},{"x":0.25,"y":0.288},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":1.386},{"x":0.9,"y":2.303},{"x":0.99,"y":4.605}]}],"annotations":[]}}
```

When the true label $y = 1$, the loss function simplifies to $-\log(p)$, heavily penalizing confident wrong guesses near zero.

Conversely, when $y = 0$, it becomes $-\log(1-p)$, heavily penalizing confident predictions near one.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy loss?
runs.title: Cross-Entropy Loss
runs.body:
Cross-entropy loss measures the performance of a classification model whose output is a probability between $0$ and $1$.

The formula for a single binary observation is $L = -y \log(p) - (1-y) \log(1-p)$, where $y$ is the true label and $p$ is the predicted probability.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Cross-entropy loss by predicted probability","caption":"Loss grows large as the prediction diverges from the true class.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Predicted probability $p$","min":0.01,"max":0.99,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Loss","min":0,"max":5},"series":[{"label":"True class 1","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":4.605},{"x":0.25,"y":1.386},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":0.288},{"x":0.99,"y":0.01}]}],"annotations":[]}}
```

When the true label $y=1$, the second term vanishes and the loss simplifies to $-\log(p)$. As the predicted probability $p$ approaches $1$, the loss drops to zero, but as $p$ nears $0$, the loss grows towards infinity.

This severe penalty for confident misclassifications drives optimization in logistic regression and neural network classifiers.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy loss?
runs.title: Cross Entropy Loss
runs.body:
Imagine a weather app trying to guess if it will rain or shine today. Cross entropy loss is a scoring rule that tells us how wrong the app's guesses are compared to reality.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Comparing Real and Predicted Labels","kind":"comparison","columns":[{"heading":"True Label","items":["Cat (1.0)","Dog (0.0)"]},{"heading":"Model Prediction","items":["Cat (0.8)","Dog (0.2)"]}]}}
```

When the app is very confident and right, the score is low and close to zero. If the app is sure it will shine when it pours, the penalty score shoots up.

We add up these surprise penalties across all our guesses to get a final grade for the model. Training the model simply means tweaking its settings to make this final penalty score as small as possible.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy loss?
runs.title: Cross Entropy Loss
runs.body:
Cross entropy loss is a way to measure how wrong a computer model is when it guesses categories. Imagine a weather app trying to guess if it will rain or shine based on today's sky.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Comparing Real Label and Model Guess","kind":"comparison","columns":[{"heading":"True Label","items":["The actual answer","Value is 1 for correct class","Value is 0 for others"]},{"heading":"Model Prediction","items":["The guessed chance","Value between 0 and 1","Total sums up to 1"]}]}}
```

The true answer is a hard fact, like 1 for rain and 0 for shine, while the model gives a percentage chance for each option.

Cross entropy loss takes these numbers and calculates a penalty score that grows much larger when the model is confident and completely wrong.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy loss?
runs.title: Cross-Entropy Loss
runs.body:
Suppose a model predicts a probability $p = 0.9$ that an image is a cat, but the true label is $y = 1$.

Cross-entropy loss measures how wrong this prediction is by taking the negative logarithm of the predicted probability for the correct class, calculated as $-\log(p)$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Cross-entropy depends on the true label","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Predicted positive probability","min":0.01,"max":0.99,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Loss","min":0,"max":5},"series":[{"label":"True class 1","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":4.605},{"x":0.1,"y":2.303},{"x":0.25,"y":1.386},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":0.288},{"x":0.9,"y":0.105},{"x":0.99,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"True class 0","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":0.01},{"x":0.1,"y":0.105},{"x":0.25,"y":0.288},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":1.386},{"x":0.9,"y":2.303},{"x":0.99,"y":4.605}]}],"annotations":[]}}
```

When the true label is $y = 1$, the loss is $-\log(p)$, which approaches zero as $p$ approaches one and skyrockets toward infinity as $p$ approaches zero.

Conversely, if the true label is $y = 0$, the loss becomes $-\log(1 - p)$, penalizing confident incorrect guesses heavily.

Summing these penalties across all classes gives the multi-class cross-entropy loss formula $-\sum y_i \log(p_i)$.

runs.prompt: what is cross entropy loss?
runs.title: Cross-entropy loss
runs.body:
Consider a model predicting whether an email is spam, outputting a probability $p = 0.9$ for a true spam email.

To measure how wrong this prediction is, we use cross-entropy loss, defined as $H(y, p) = -y \log p - (1-y) \log(1-p)$ for true label $y$ and predicted probability $p$.

This formula penalizes confident wrong answers heavily by taking the negative logarithm of the predicted probability assigned to the correct class.

Look at the curves in to see how loss spikes toward infinity as predictions become confidently incorrect.


When the true label $y=1$, the loss function simplifies to $-\log p$.

runs.prompt: what is batch normalization?
runs.title: Batch Normalization
runs.body:
Batch normalization stabilizes deep neural networks by normalizing layer inputs across a mini-batch. Look at the transformation diagram to see how raw activations become standardized values.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Normalize layer inputs","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Original activations","items":["Unstable variance","Shifting distributions"]},"after":{"label":"Normalized outputs","items":["Mean zero","Unit variance"]},"operation":"Subtract batch mean, divide by standard deviation, then scale and shift"}}
```

For each mini-batch, the network computes the mean and variance to adjust the activations. Two learnable parameters, scale and shift, allow the model to retain its expressive power.

runs.prompt: what is batch normalization?
runs.title: Batch Normalization
runs.body:
Batch normalization is a technique for training deep neural networks faster and more reliably. It stabilizes the learning process by re-centering and re-scaling layer inputs.

Look at the diagram below to see how raw activations transform into normalized outputs.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Batch normalization step","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Input batch","items":["Layer activations $x_i$"]},"after":{"label":"Normalized output","items":["Scaled and shifted $y_i$"]},"operation":"Subtract mean $\\mu_B$, divide by variance $\\sigma_B$, then apply $\\gamma$ and $\\beta$"}}
```

During training, the network computes the mean and variance for each mini-batch of data. It normalizes the activations so they maintain a mean of zero and a variance of one.

Two learnable parameters, gamma and beta, allow the network to scale and shift the normalized values as needed. This prevents the training process from getting bogged down by shifting value distributions across layers.

runs.prompt: how does dropout work?
runs.title: Dropout in Neural Networks
runs.body:
Dropout prevents neural networks from overfitting by randomly turning off hidden units during training.

Each unit is retained with a fixed probability $p$, forcing the network to learn redundant representations across different paths.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Dropout transformation","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"All units active","items":["h1","h2","h3"]},"after":{"label":"Sampled mask","items":["h1","dropped","h3"]},"operation":"Randomly zero units with probability 1 - p"}}
```

In the diagram above, notice how the second unit is temporarily removed for a single training step. At test time, all units remain active, but their weights are scaled by $p$ to match the expected activation values.

runs.prompt: how does dropout work?
runs.title: How Dropout Works
runs.body:
Dropout prevents neural networks from overfitting by randomly silencing neurons during training.

For every training step, each hidden unit is dropped with probability $1-p$, breaking complex co-adaptations between features.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Dropout transformation","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Training Forward Pass","items":["All hidden units active","Full activation vector"]},"after":{"label":"Masked Forward Pass","items":["Random units zeroed out","Rescaled activations"]},"operation":"Apply Bernoulli mask with probability p"}}
```

During inference, all units remain active, but their incoming weights are multiplied by the keep rate $p$ to match the expected value from training.

This simple mechanism acts as an ensemble method, averaging over exponentially many sub-networks.

runs.prompt: how does cross-validation detect overfitting?
runs.title: Cross-Validation and Overfitting
runs.body:
Overfitting happens when a model learns noise in the training data rather than the true underlying pattern, performing poorly on unseen examples.

Cross-validation splits data into folds, training on some and testing on others, to measure generalisation error honestly.

Observe the gap in error rates shown in the chart below to understand how the discrepancy exposes memorisation.


When training error drops much lower than cross-validation error, the model has overfitted the specific samples it saw.

This gap acts as a reliable warning signal that your model lacks generalisation.

In the sentence The cat sat on the mat, a single attention mechanism struggles to track both syntactic structure and semantic ties at the exact same time.

Multi-head attention solves this by splitting the representation into separate subspaces, allowing different heads to specialize in distinct linguistic relations.

Meanwhile, Head B attends more broadly to determiners or distant objects, learning different facets of the sequence context.

runs.prompt: How does a transformer get a match score between words?
runs.title: Transformer Word Match Scores
runs.body:
Transformers compute match scores between words using vector dot products inside the self-attention mechanism.

When processing a sentence, each word takes on a query representation and a key representation through learned linear projections.

To find how much focus a query word should place on every other word, the model multiplies the query vector by each key vector.

Look for the raw dot products in the matrix where the query sat meets keys like cat and sat itself.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Query-Key dot products and scaled scores","caption":"Compare the query for sat with each key, then divide by the square root of key width.","kind":"matrix","columns":["Dot product","Scaled score"],"rows":[{"heading":"the 1","cells":["-0.539","-0.381"]},{"heading":"cat 2","cells":["3.034","2.145"]},{"heading":"sat 3","cells":["1.306","0.923"]}]}}
```

Because large vector dimensions push dot products to extreme values where gradients vanish, transformers divide each raw score by the square root of the key dimension.

runs.prompt: How does a transformer get a match score between words?
runs.title: Word Matching in Transformers via Attention
runs.body:
Transformers compute match scores between words using vector dot products. When processing a sentence, each word takes on three roles: a query, a key, and a value.

The model takes the dot product of a word's query vector with all other words' key vectors to find alignment.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Scaled Attention Scores between Words","caption":"Compare query vectors with key vectors and divide by key width square root.","kind":"matrix","layout":"teaching","columns":["Dot Product","Scaled Score"],"rows":[{"id":"k1","heading":"the","cells":["-0.54","—"]},{"id":"k2","heading":"cat","cells":["3.03","—"]},{"id":"k3","heading":"sat","cells":["1.31","—"]},{"id":"k4","heading":"on","cells":["-0.36","—"]}]}}
```

These raw dot products grow too large for high dimensions, pushing softmax into flat regions with tiny gradients.

To prevent this instability, the model scales down the products by dividing them by the square root of the key vector dimension.

The resulting scaled scores determine how much focus each word places on others during the attention step.

Once a transformer computes attention weights, it multiplies each value vector by its corresponding scalar weight and sums the results together.

This operation blends the contextual representation so that words with higher relevance contribute more to the output token vector.

For instance, in the phrase the cat sat on the mat, the target word sat might assign a weight of $0.65$ to cat and $0.192$ to sat itself.

Looking at the block stack, each token's value vector is scaled by its attention probability before aggregation. The final combined vector is the weighted sum across all contributing positions in the sequence.

This linear combination allows the model to gather information from relevant context words dynamically.

runs.prompt: how does cross-validation detect overfitting?
runs.title: Detecting Overfitting with Cross-Validation
runs.body:
Cross-validation detects overfitting by partitioning data into $k$ folds, training on $k-1$ folds, and evaluating on the held-out fold iteratively.

This yields an out-of-sample error estimate that reflects generalisation performance on unseen data.

Observe how validation error diverges from training error as complexity increases in the plot below.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Error by model complexity","caption":"Validation error rises as training error falls, exposing overfit complexity.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Model complexity","min":1,"max":5},"y":{"label":"Error rate","min":0,"max":0.5},"series":[{"label":"Training error","kind":"line","points":[{"x":1,"y":0.4},{"x":2,"y":0.25},{"x":3,"y":0.15},{"x":4,"y":0.08},{"x":5,"y":0.02}]},{"label":"Validation error","kind":"line","points":[{"x":1,"y":0.42},{"x":2,"y":0.28},{"x":3,"y":0.2},{"x":4,"y":0.25},{"x":5,"y":0.38}]}]}}
```

When a model memorizes training noise rather than learning true underlying patterns, training error continues to drop while validation error increases.

By averaging validation scores across all $k$ splits, cross-validation exposes this divergence reliably without wasting precious data.

runs.prompt: how does cross-validation detect overfitting?
runs.title: Detecting Overfitting with Cross-Validation
runs.body:
Cross-validation detects overfitting by partitioning data into $k$ folds, training on $k-1$ folds, and evaluating on the held-out fold.

This rotates the validation fold $k$ times to yield an unbiased estimate of generalisation error.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Training versus validation error across model complexity","caption":"Illustrative error rates showing validation error rising when a complex model overfits.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Model complexity","min":1,"max":9,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Error rate","min":0,"max":0.5},"series":[{"label":"Training error","kind":"line","points":[{"x":1,"y":0.35},{"x":3,"y":0.2},{"x":5,"y":0.1},{"x":7,"y":0.04},{"x":9,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"Validation error","kind":"line","points":[{"x":1,"y":0.38},{"x":3,"y":0.22},{"x":5,"y":0.15},{"x":7,"y":0.28},{"x":9,"y":0.42}]}]}}
```

When training error drops near zero while validation error reverses and increases, cross-validation exposes the divergence.

The formula for $k$-fold cross-validation error is $E_{CV} = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i=1}^{k} L(y_i, f_{-i}(x_i))$.

In practice, data leakage across folds causes overly optimistic performance estimates. Proper cross-validation requires isolating all preprocessing steps inside each fold loop.

The exact formula is $\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}})V$, where $d_k$ is the key dimension. These weights represent the proportional relevance of each source token to the query token.

It also places a notable weight of $0.2$ on mat, capturing the locative object of the clause.

runs.title: Causal Masking in Transformer Decoder
runs.body:
The decoder computes attention scores for each query token against all key tokens. To prevent using future information, a causal mask adds $-\,\infty$ to any score where the key index $j$ exceeds the query index $i$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"kind":"heatmap","title":"Causal mask before softmax","caption":"Gray cells are blocked (‑∞) so later keys get zero weight.","rowLabel":"Query position","columnLabel":"Key position","columns":["1","2","3","4","5","6"],"rows":[{"label":"1","cells":[null,null,null,null,null,null]},{"label":"2","cells":[0,null,null,null,null,null]},{"label":"3","cells":[0,0,null,null,null,null]},{"label":"4","cells":[0,0,0,null,null,null]},{"label":"5","cells":[0,0,0,0,null,null]},{"label":"6","cells":[0,0,0,0,0,null]}],"range":{"min":0,"max":1}}}
```

After adding the mask, the softmax normalises only the allowed scores, yielding a probability distribution that sums to 1 for each row. Consequently, each token can attend only to itself and earlier tokens.

The mask is a binary matrix: entry $(i,j)$ is 0 (allowed) when $j\le i$ and $-\infty$ (blocked) otherwise. This simple rule enforces the autoregressive property required for language generation.

This mechanism solves the bottleneck of compressed fixed-length context vectors by providing direct access to all encoder hidden states.

Transformers use multi-head attention to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions.

Single-head attention averages out these diverse relational roles, limiting the model's capacity to capture syntax and semantics simultaneously.

By splitting the query, key, and value vectors into $h$ separate subspaces, each head projects inputs via distinct weight matrices $W_i^Q, W_i^K, W_i^V$.

runs.prompt: How does a transformer get a match score between words?
runs.title: Transformer Word Match Scores
runs.body:
Transformers compute match scores between words using the dot product of query and key vectors. For any query vector $q$ and key vector $k_j$, the raw alignment score is given by their inner product $q \cdot k_j$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Scaled dot-product scores for sat","caption":"Use $s_j=(q\\cdot k_j)/\\sqrt{d_k}$ for each key, with $d_k=2$ shown out of 256 entries.","kind":"matrix","layout":"teaching","columns":["Dot product","Scaled score"],"rows":[{"id":"k1","heading":"the 1","cells":["-0.539","-0.381"]},{"id":"k2","heading":"cat 2","cells":["3.034","2.145"]},{"id":"k3","heading":"sat 3","cells":["1.306","0.923"]}]}}
```

To prevent large dimension sizes from pushing softmax functions into regions with extremely small gradients, models scale these dot products down.

The scaled dot-product attention formula divides each score by the square root of the key dimension $\sqrt{d_k}$.

Thus, the final match score becomes $s_j = \frac{q \cdot k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}$. This scaling stabilizes training and ensures that gradient updates remain effective across varying layer widths.

runs.prompt: How does a transformer get a match score between words?
runs.title: Scaled dot-product attention scores
runs.body:
Transformers compute match scores between words using the dot product of query and key vectors. For a given query $q$ and key $k_j$, the raw score is $q \cdot k_j$.

To prevent gradients from vanishing in the softmax function when dimensions are large, this raw product is scaled down.

The final score formula is $s_j = \frac{q \cdot k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}$, where $d_k$ is the dimensionality of the key vectors.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Scaled dot-product scores for sat","caption":"Use $s_j=(q\\cdot k_j)/\\sqrt{d_k}$ for each key, with $d_k=2$ shown out of 256 entries.","kind":"matrix","layout":"teaching","columns":["Dot product","Scaled score"],"rows":[{"id":"k1","heading":"the 1","cells":["-0.539","-0.381"]},{"id":"k2","heading":"cat 2","cells":["3.034","2.145"]},{"id":"k3","heading":"sat 3","cells":["1.306","0.923"]},{"id":"k4","heading":"on 4","cells":["-0.361","-0.255"]},{"id":"k5","heading":"the 5","cells":["-1.924","-1.36"]},{"id":"k6","heading":"mat 6","cells":["-1.486","-1.051"]}]}}
```

As shown in the matrix above, dividing by the square root of $d_k$ shrinks large magnitudes. This keeps the variance stable at $1$ when components have unit variance.

Without this scaling, high dimensional dot products grow too large and push softmax into regions with near-zero gradients.

runs.prompt: How does a transformer mix the word values after it has attention weights?
runs.title: Mixing Word Values With Attention Weights
runs.body:
Once attention weights are computed, the transformer mixes all value vectors by taking their weighted sum. Look at the block stack in to see each word vector scaled by its attention weight before they are added together.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Weighted values for sat","kind":"block-stack","orientation":"horizontal","blocks":[{"id":"a","label":"the 0.052","diagram":{"kind":"tensor","tensor":{"rows":1,"columns":2,"dimensions":"256","values":[0.2,1.4]}}},{"id":"b","label":"cat 0.65","diagram":{"kind":"tensor","tensor":{"rows":1,"columns":2,"dimensions":"256","values":[0.31,1]}}},{"id":"c","label":"sat 0.192","diagram":{"kind":"tensor","tensor":{"rows":1,"columns":2,"dimensions":"256","values":[0.72,1.4]}}},{"id":"d","label":"on 0.059","diagram":{"kind":"tensor","tensor":{"rows":1,"columns":2,"dimensions":"256","values":[-0.17,1.2]}}}]}}
```

The operation computes the output vector $z$ via the formula $z = \sum_j a_j v_j$, where $a_j$ is the attention weight and $v_j$ is the value vector for token $j$.

This linear combination merges context from all relevant positions into a single representation.

A primary failure mode of this mixing step is over-smoothing, where high attention weights distributed uniformly across too many unrelated tokens cause the output vectors to lose distinct token identities.

runs.prompt: How does a transformer mix the word values after it has attention weights?
runs.title: Mixing Word Values via Attention Weights
runs.body:
Once attention weights are computed, the transformer mixes the word vectors by calculating a weighted sum.

Look at the weighted value tensors in the diagram to see how each vector is scaled by its attention weight before combination.

runs.prompt: what is maximum likelihood estimation?
runs.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation
runs.body:
Maximum likelihood estimation finds parameter values that maximize the likelihood function for observed data.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Likelihood function $L(\\theta)$","caption":"The maximum likelihood estimate $\\hat{\\theta}$ maximizes the probability of observing the data.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Parameter $\\theta$","min":0,"max":10},"y":{"label":"Likelihood $L(\\theta)$","min":0,"max":1},"series":[{"label":"$L(\\theta)$","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0.1},{"x":2,"y":0.4},{"x":4,"y":0.8},{"x":5,"y":0.95,"label":"$\\hat{\\theta}$"},{"x":6,"y":0.85},{"x":8,"y":0.4},{"x":10,"y":0.1}]}]}}
```

The estimator solves $\hat{\theta} = \arg\max_{\theta} L(\theta)$, equivalent to maximizing the log-likelihood $\ln L(\theta)$.

A key limit in practice is computational intractability when the likelihood lacks a closed-form derivative.

runs.prompt: what is maximum likelihood estimation?
runs.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation
runs.body:
Maximum likelihood estimation finds parameter values that maximize the likelihood function for observed data.

Given independent and identically distributed data $x_1, \dots, x_n$ from a density $f(x; \theta)$, the joint likelihood is $L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i; \theta)$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Likelihood function for parameter $\\theta$","caption":"The maximum likelihood estimate $\\hat{\\theta}$ maximizes the likelihood $L(\\theta|x)$ of observing data $x$.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Parameter $\\theta$","min":0,"max":10},"y":{"label":"Likelihood $L(\\theta)$","min":0,"max":1},"series":[{"label":"$L(\\theta)$","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0.1},{"x":2,"y":0.4},{"x":4,"y":0.8},{"x":5,"y":1,"label":"$\\hat{\\theta}$"},{"x":6,"y":0.8},{"x":8,"y":0.3},{"x":10,"y":0.05}]}]}}
```

In practice, we maximize the log-likelihood function $l(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log f(x_i; \theta)$ instead of the product.

Setting the derivative to zero yields the score equation $\frac{\partial l}{\theta} = 0$, which solves for the estimator $\hat{\theta}$.

Under mild regularity conditions, maximum likelihood estimators are asymptotically unbiased and achieve the Cramér-Rao lower bound, making them statistically efficient.

For each threshold, the algorithm sorts the feature values and computes the midpoint between adjacent unique points.

It splits the data into two subsets, left and right, and measures the impurity of each using the Gini impurity formula. The weighted average of these impurities forms the score for that candidate cut.

To pick the best split, the tree compares all candidate scores and selects the threshold that minimizes impurity.

runs.prompt: why does a bootstrap sample contain only about 63% of the unique training rows?
runs.title: Why a Bootstrap Sample Covers 63 Percent of Rows
runs.body:
When we build a bootstrap sample of size $n$, we draw rows with replacement from our original dataset. Notice how the chance that any specific row is picked on a single draw is $\frac{1}{n}$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Bootstrap coverage limit","caption":"Worked example. Omission with replacement is $(1-1/n)^n$. Limit $1/e\\approx 0.368$ gives expected coverage $1-0.368=0.632$.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Training rows n","min":1,"max":10,"integerTicks":true},"y":{"label":"Chance a row is omitted","min":0,"max":0.5},"series":[{"label":"Omission after n draws","kind":"line","points":[{"x":1,"y":0},{"x":2,"y":0.25},{"x":3,"y":0.296},{"x":4,"y":0.316},{"x":5,"y":0.328},{"x":6,"y":0.335},{"x":7,"y":0.34},{"x":8,"y":0.344},{"x":9,"y":0.346},{"x":10,"y":0.349}]}],"annotations":[{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Omission limit","axis":"y","value":0.368}]}}
```

That means the probability of missing that row on one draw is $1 - \frac{1}{n}$. Because all $n$ draws are independent, the probability that the row is omitted from the entire bootstrap sample is $(1 - \frac{1}{n})^n$.

As $n$ grows larger, this expression approaches the mathematical constant $e$, so the omission rate converges to $\frac{1}{e}$, which is approximately $0.368$.

The expected unique coverage is the exact complement of this omission rate, giving $1 - 0.368$, or about $63.2\%$.

runs.prompt: why does a bootstrap sample contain only about 63% of the unique training rows?

runs.body:
When we draw a sample of size $n$ with replacement from a dataset of $n$ rows, each draw has a $\frac{1}{n}$ chance of picking any specific row.

The probability that a single row is not chosen on one draw is therefore $1 - \frac{1}{n}$.

```rh-diagram

Limit $1/e≈0.368$ gives expected coverage $1-0.368=0.632$.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Training rows n","min":1,"max":20,"integerTicks":true},"y":{"label":"Chance a row is omitted","min":0,"max":0.4},"series":[{"label":"Omission after n draws","kind":"line","samples":{"x":{"start":1,"step":1},"y":[0,250,296,316,328,335,340,344,346,349,350,352,353,354,355,356,357,357,358,358],"divisor":1000}}],"annotations":[{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Omission limit","axis":"y","value":0.368}]}}
```

Because all $n$ draws are independent events, the chance that a specific row escapes being picked across all $n$ trials is $(1 - \frac{1}{n})^n$.

As $n$ grows large, this expression approaches the mathematical constant $e^{-1}$, which is approximately $0.368$ or $36.8\%$.

Since about $36.8\%$ of the original rows are left out of a bootstrap sample, the remaining unique rows that do get included make up the complement, which is $1 - 0.368 = 0.632$ or about $63\%$.

runs.prompt: how does Gini impurity change as the fraction of one class goes from 0 to 1, compared with entropy?
runs.title: Gini impurity and entropy
runs.body:
When building a decision tree, nodes split data based on metrics like Gini impurity and entropy to measure node purity.

As the fraction of one class $p$ goes from $0$ to $1$, both metrics start at zero, reach a peak at an even split, and drop back to zero.

Gini impurity calculates the probability of incorrectly classifying a randomly chosen element. For a binary split, it follows the formula $G(p) = 2p(1-p)$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Gini impurity and entropy","caption":"Worked example. G(p)=2p(1-p) and H(p)=-p log_2 p-(1-p) log_2(1-p). runs.title: Gini Impurity and Information Gain
```
runs.body:
To measure node purity, we compute the Gini impurity as $1 - \sum p_i^2$, where $p_i$ is the probability of class $i$.

Consider a root node split into two equal halves where the left child has 4 items of class 0 and 0 of class 1, and the right has 1 of class 0 and 3 of class 1.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Gini after the root split","caption":"Worked example. Combine the child Ginis in proportion to their sizes.","kind":"matrix","columns":["Class 0","Class 1","Gini","Weight"],"rows":[{"heading":"Left","cells":["4","0","0","0.5"]},{"heading":"Right","cells":["1","3","0.375","0.5"]},{"heading":"After","cells":["—","—","0.1875","1"]}]}}
```

Notice how the left child's impurity is zero because it is pure, while the right child yields $1 - (1/4)^2 - (3/4)^2 = 0.375$.

We then compute the weighted average of the child impurities to find the split's total impurity, which is $0.5(0) + 0.5(0.375) = 0.1875$.

Information gain is the reduction in impurity, found by subtracting this split impurity from the parent node's impurity.

runs.title: Computing Gini Impurity and Gain
runs.body:
Consider a node with four samples of class 0 and four of class 1. A candidate split yields a left child with four items of class 0 and zero of class 1, and a right child with one item of class 0 and three of class 1.

We compute impurity using $1 - \sum p_i^2$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Gini after the root split","caption":"Worked example. Combine the child Ginis in proportion to their sizes.","kind":"matrix","columns":["Class 0","Class 1","Gini","Weight"],"rows":[{"heading":"Left","cells":["4","0","0","0.5"]},{"heading":"Right","cells":["1","3","0.375","0.5"]},{"heading":"After","cells":["—","—","0.1875","1"]}]}}
```

For the left child, all items belong to class 0, giving a Gini impurity of zero.

For the right child, the probabilities are $\frac{1}{4}$ and $\frac{3}{4}$, resulting in a Gini impurity of $1 - ((\frac{1}{4})^2 + (\frac{3}{4})^2) = 0.375$.

We then calculate the weighted average impurity of the children, which is $0.5 \times 0 + 0.5 \times 0.375 = 0.1875$.

runs.prompt: How does a transformer turn scores into a guess for the next word?
runs.title: Turning Scores Into Words
runs.body:
After processing a sequence, the model projects its internal state through a linear layer to produce raw scores called logits for each candidate in its vocabulary.

Look at the bar chart to see how each candidate word receives a unique logit score before normalization. For example, the word on receives a high score of $1.745$ compared to negative scores for unlikely words.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Vocabulary logits after the cat sat","caption":"A linear layer gives each word in the toy vocabulary a raw score.","kind":"bar-chart","bars":[{"label":"the","value":0.501},{"label":"cat","value":-0.108},{"label":"sat","value":0.78},{"label":"on","value":1.745},{"label":"mat","value":0.201},{"label":"slept","value":-0.495}]}}
```

These raw scores are then processed by a softmax function to turn them into valid probabilities that sum to one. This mathematical operation exponentiates each logit and divides by the sum of all exponentiated values.

The highest resulting probability determines the final guessed word for the next position in the sequence.

Cross-entropy loss computes the penalty by taking the negative log probability assigned to the correct choice.

Because the target vector is sparse, all incorrect options with a target of zero are ignored during the summation.

The model updates its weights by pushing the predicted share of the correct token closer to one and suppressing all other items.
